figures.title: AlexNet Architecture
figures.caption: **AlexNet Architecture**: Two parallel GPU streams process $224{\times}224$ input images through convolutional layers (green blocks) that extract spatial features at decreasing resolutions, converging through three fully connected layers to 1,000 output classes. Because each stream holds half of the network, the figure also shows how the model was partitioned across two GPUs. Adapted from @krizhevsky2012imagenet.
figures.alt: 3D diagram of AlexNet with two parallel GPU streams. Green blocks show convolutional layers decreasing from 224x224 input. Red kernels overlay green blocks. Right side shows three dense layers converging to 1000 outputs.

figures.title: The Era of Scale
figures.caption: **The Era of Scale**: Each point plots a third-party training-compute estimate (FLOPs) for a notable model against its publication year on a log scale. Runs below $10^{22}$ FLOPs appear in blue; larger runs appear in red. The dashed line is a least-squares fit to these points and doubles every `{python} TrainingComputeGrowthFigure.doubling_months_str` months. From AlexNet (2012) to GPT-4-class training scale (2023), compute requirements increased by roughly `{python} TrainingComputeGrowthFigure.compute_growth_order_str` orders of magnitude (about `{python} TrainingComputeGrowthFigure.compute_growth_m_str` times). This endpoint comparison is distinct from training-compute trend studies [@amodei2018aicompute; @sevilla2022] and is used here to motivate the specialized infrastructure described in this book. Data from Epoch AI's Notable AI Models database [@epochai2026notable].
figures.alt: Scatter plot of training-compute estimates on a logarithmic scale from 2012 to 2025. Blue points mark runs below 10 to the 22 FLOPs; red points mark larger runs. A dashed least-squares fit line rises through the points.

figures.title: Fifty Years of Microprocessor Trends
figures.caption: **Fifty Years of Microprocessor Trends**: Transistor count, single-thread performance (SPECint benchmark score), clock frequency, typical power, and logical core count of microprocessors from 1971 to 2021 on a logarithmic axis. Transistor counts keep rising after the mid-2000s while frequency and typical power level off and single-thread performance slows; the gray band marks the end of Dennard scaling, after which added transistors went into more cores. Data from @rupp2022microprocessor.
figures.alt: Scatter plot on a logarithmic vertical axis from 1970 to 2022 with five series: transistors in thousands rising steadily to about 10 to the 7.7, single-thread performance rising and then flattening after about 2005, frequency in megahertz flattening near 3,000 to 5,000 after 2005, typical power in watts leveling near 100, and logical cores staying at 1 until about 2005 and then rising. A gray vertical band near 2005 is labeled end of Dennard scaling.

figures.title: Smart Doorbell Constraint Scorecard
figures.caption: **Smart Doorbell Constraint Scorecard**: Each bar is demand over supply, so the dashed line marks the point where a level is exactly saturated. The model occupies a small fraction of the ESP32-S3's 4 MB flash budget (Level 1: PASS), but its 101 ms latency (25 MFLOP of compute plus fixed overhead) is twice a tightened 50 ms budget for a responsive chime (Level 2: FAIL), even though it clears the scenario's canonical 200 ms budget.
figures.alt: Horizontal bar chart of demand over supply with a dashed saturation line at 1.0. The latency (SLA) bar is red and extends to about twice the line. The memory (flash) bar is green and short, far below the line.

figures.title: ETL vs. ELT Architectural Paradigms

figures.title: From Neuron to Machine
figures.caption: **From Neuron to Machine**: One neuron is a dot product between an input row and a weight column. A layer applied to a batch stacks those dot products into one matrix multiply whose cost is the product of batch size, input width, and output width. On an accelerator, a tile of the weight matrix stays inside an array of multiply-accumulate units while input rows stream through, so the batch, not the neuron, sets how much arithmetic each fetched weight pays for.
figures.alt: Three panels left to right. One neuron: a horizontal input bar of size 1 by n-in times a vertical weight bar of size n-in by 1, labeled a dot product of n-in MACs. One layer, one batch: matrix X of size B by n-in times W of size n-in by n-out equals Z of size B by n-out, labeled B times n-in times n-out MACs. On the machine: four input rows stream into a four-by-four grid of green multiply-accumulate cells holding a weight tile, producing Z on the right; caption says each weight is fetched once and reused by all B rows.
figures.systems_goal: Show how batching amortizes weight-tile fetches over multiple input rows.

figures.visual: Retain the existing figure, geometry, labels, color roles, and unchanged caption. Three panels left to right. One layer, one batch: matrix X of size B by n-in times W of size n-in by n-out equals Z of size B by n-out, labeled B times n-in times n-out MACs. figures.title: Cross-Entropy Compares a Distribution with a One-Hot Label
figures.caption: **Cross-Entropy Compares a Distribution with a One-Hot Label**: Left: the network places 0.8 on the correct class and 0.1 each on digits 0 and 9, while the target places all of its mass on the correct class. figures.title: The Efficiency Frontier
figures.caption: **The Efficiency Frontier**: ImageNet top-1 accuracy plotted against computational cost in GMACs per image. Representative points are compiled from published model reports for AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, Inception, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, ViT, Swin Transformer, and ConvNeXt [@krizhevsky2012imagenet; @simonyan2014very; @he2016; @szegedy2015; @sandler2018; @tan2019efficientnet; @dosovitskiy2021image; @liu2021swin; @liu2022convnet]. The dashed Pareto frontier is an illustrative trade-off curve rather than a benchmark rerun; exact accuracy and reported compute values vary by model variant, training recipe, implementation, and operation-counting convention (multiply-accumulates vs. floating-point operations). The legend distinguishes six families: legacy CNNs (gray), dense CNNs (blue), efficient Mobile architectures (green), EfficientNet-class models (violet), modern CNNs (orange), and Transformers (red). The frontier is led by the efficient and modern-CNN families; the Transformers trade substantial compute for flexible long-range modeling without dominating it, and ViT-B/16 sits below the frontier. AlexNet is the single-model result, and ViT-B/16 is plotted at the 384-pixel resolution at which its accuracy was measured.
figures.alt: Scatter plot of ImageNet top-1 accuracy against compute cost on a logarithmic horizontal axis. Ten labeled model points use six colors for architecture families, and a gray dashed line connects MobileNetV2, EfficientNet-B0, ConvNeXt-T, and EfficientNet-B7.

figures.caption: **Multilayer Perceptron Architecture**: A three-layer network in which every neuron connects to all neurons in adjacent layers. figures.title: Residual Connection Block (Original Post-Activation Form)
figures.caption: **Residual Connection Block (Original Post-Activation Form)**: The original ResNet block [@he2016] implements $\ResidualBlockOutput = \text{ReLU}(\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \LayerInputVector)$, where an identity shortcut bypasses the weight layers before a final ReLU activation. In later pre-activation variants [@he2016identity] and modern transformer blocks, the nonlinearity moves inside $\ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector)$, making the addition a completely clean identity shortcut $\ResidualBlockOutput = \ResidualFunction(\LayerInputVector) + \LayerInputVector$ that matches the unobstructed gradient flow in @eq-residual.
figures.alt: Two blue weight layer blocks with ReLU between them. An input vector enters left, passes through the weight layers, then adds with an identity shortcut that bypasses both layers. Brown plus circle combines paths. Output shows the residual sum with final ReLU.

figures.title: Recurrent Neural Network Unfolding
figures.caption: **Recurrent Neural Network Unfolding**: The compact recurrent loop (left) unfolds into one copy of the cell per time step (right). Three weight matrices are shared across all steps: $\RecurrentInputWeights$ (input-to-hidden), $\RecurrentStateWeights$ (hidden-to-hidden), and $\RecurrentOutputWeights$ (hidden-to-output). These matrices are reused at every step, so the parameter count is independent of sequence length. For a 128-dimensional hidden state and a 100-dimensional input, each time step requires 16,384 MACs for recurrent connections plus 12,800 for input projection.
figures.alt: Left: single green hidden node with a hidden-to-hidden self-loop. Right: unfolded across three time steps showing purple inputs, green hidden states, and orange outputs. Arrows show shared input-to-hidden, hidden-to-hidden, and hidden-to-output weights across all steps.

figures.title: Transformer Architecture (Encoder-Decoder)
figures.caption: **Transformer Architecture (Encoder-Decoder)**: The encoder (left, repeated $\LayerCount$ times) consists of multi-head attention followed by feed-forward layers, each with residual connections (arrows bypassing blocks) and layer normalization. The decoder (right) adds masked attention to prevent attending to future tokens during training and autoregressive generation. Positional encodings (sine waves) inject sequence order information absent from the permutation-equivariant attention operation. This design enables training parallelism across all positions while the decoder maintains autoregressive causality during inference. Adapted from @vaswani2017.
figures.alt: Encoder-decoder architecture. Encoder: multi-head attention, add-norm, feed-forward, add-norm, repeated N_L times. Decoder adds masked attention. Positional encoding sine waves at inputs. Skip connections bypass sublayers. Linear and softmax at top.

figures.title: Prefill and Decode
figures.caption: **Prefill and Decode**: Prefill (left) runs the whole prompt through the model in one pass of matrix-matrix products, reusing every weight across all prompt tokens, and writes each prompt token's keys and values to the KV cache. Decode (right) then generates one token per step: each output becomes the next input, each step runs matrix-vector products that re-read every weight, and each step reads the whole cache and appends one entry. The first phase is usually compute-bound; the second is usually bandwidth-bound at small batch.
figures.alt: Left panel labeled Prefill: four blue prompt tokens, The, cat, sat, on, feed one wide box labeled one pass over all prompt tokens (matrix-matrix products), which writes four orange KV cache cells. An arrow leads to the right panel labeled Decode: three narrow boxes labeled one token (matrix-vector), each taking a green token (the, mat, today) and producing the next (mat, today, end), with dashed arrows showing each output becoming the next input; each box reads the cache and adds one orange cell. Captions beneath read: weights reused across every prompt token, usually compute-bound; and every weight and the whole cache re-read for each new token, usually bandwidth-bound at small batch.

figures.title: Three Memory Regimes of a Long Context
figures.caption: **Three Memory Regimes of a Long Context**: Memory against context length for a model with GPT-2 XL's shape (48 layers, width 1,600, 25 heads) in FP16, evaluated past its trained context to expose the scaling. The weights are fixed, the KV cache that serving keeps for one request grows linearly, and a single layer's materialized attention scores grow quadratically. The cache overtakes the weights near `{python} ContextMemoryCrossings.kv_crossing_tokens_str`, and one layer's scores alone would fill one accelerator's device memory near `{python} ContextMemoryCrossings.score_crossing_tokens_str`, which is why tiled attention avoids materializing them.

A dashed red line for one layer's materialized scores rises quadratically and crosses a dotted line for one accelerator's device memory near 41K tokens.

figures.title: Data Movement Primitives
figures.caption: **Data Movement Primitives**: Four fundamental patterns govern information flow in neural network computation. Broadcast (top-left) replicates a single value to all destinations, used when sharing weights across batch elements. Scatter (top-right) distributes distinct elements to different destinations, enabling work partitioning. Gather (bottom-left) collects distributed values to a single location, as in attention pooling. Reduction (bottom-right) combines multiple values through aggregation (sum, max), appearing in gradient synchronization and attention scoring. Because moving data costs more than computing on it, these patterns are primary optimization targets.
figures.alt: Four diagrams with nodes and arrows. Broadcast: one red square to four nodes. Scatter: four colored squares to four nodes. Gather: four nodes with colored squares to one. Reduction: four nodes labeled 1, 3, 5, and 7 combine into one node labeled 16.

figures.title: Tensor Memory Layout
figures.caption: **Tensor Memory Layout**: A $2{\times}3$ tensor can be stored in linear memory using either row-major (C-style) or column-major (Fortran-style) ordering. Strides count elements skipped in each dimension, so i $\times$ stride[0] + j $\times$ stride[1] gives an element offset. Multiplying by the element size gives the byte offset from the storage origin. The choice of layout affects which traversals access neighboring elements efficiently.
figures.alt: Left: 2×3 tensor grid with values 1–6. Right: two linear arrays showing row-major layout (1,2,3,4,5,6) and column-major layout (1,4,2,5,3,6). Below: stride calculations for row-major [3,1] and column-major [1,2].

figures.title: ResNet-50 Data Path on One H100
figures.caption: **ResNet-50 Data Path on One H100**: One ImageNet epoch crosses four stages: local storage, host decoding and augmentation, the PCIe link, and the accelerator. Loads under each stage are per full epoch at the compute-bound rate; notes above each stage name the lever that acts there. A materialized coreset halves the storage read and the arithmetic, stream-and-discard filtering halves only the arithmetic, offline distillation targets add bytes to every stage before the accelerator, and a scoring pass adds one third of an epoch of forward arithmetic once. The host stage, outlined in red, must decode and augment every image at the accelerator's rate.

The host box has a thick red outline and a red note that it must keep pace with the accelerator. Above each box a colored note names the selection lever that acts on that stage.

figures.title: Distributed Coreset Selection Architecture
figures.caption: **Distributed Coreset Selection Architecture**: Parallel shard-local scoring reduces the work assigned to a centralized rank-merging coordinator. Workers send local EL2N scores upward; the coordinator merges them and broadcasts final coreset indices. All boxes are processes on one host; the coordinator is a selection role, and each worker drives one accelerator. The design is beneficial only when this coordination overhead remains below the training time saved by the coreset.
figures.alt: Architecture diagram with one wide Coordinator Node above three representative worker boxes labeled Worker 0, Worker 1, and Worker N, separated by ellipses. The coordinator lists a global FAISS embedding index, merged local selections, and broadcast final coreset indices. Paired arrows show local scores flowing upward from workers and final coreset indices flowing downward.

figures.title: Low-Rank Factorization
figures.caption: **Low-Rank Factorization**: A weight matrix $\WeightMatrix$ of size $\WeightMatrixRowCount{\times}\WeightMatrixColumnCount$ is approximated by two smaller factors, $\LowRankLeftFactor$ $(\WeightMatrixRowCount{\times}\FactorizationRank)$ and $\LowRankRightFactor^T$ $(\FactorizationRank{\times}\WeightMatrixColumnCount)$. figures.title: Floating-Point Bit Layouts
figures.caption: **Floating-Point Bit Layouts**: Bit allocation trades dynamic range against significand precision. FP32 uses 8 exponent and 23 fraction bits. BF16 retains FP32's 8-bit exponent and therefore a similar numerical range, but reduces the fraction to 7 bits. FP16 uses 5 exponent and 10 fraction bits, providing more significand precision than BF16 but a narrower range that can require loss scaling during training.
figures.alt: Three horizontal bit-layout diagrams. FP32 shows 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 fraction bits. FP16 shows 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, and 10 fraction bits. BF16 shows 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 7 fraction bits.

actual_steps.title: Spend more FP16 bits on the fraction
actual_steps.description: FP16 uses five exponent bits and ten fraction bits. Its narrower exponent range can make small training updates underflow, motivating loss scaling.

actual_steps.title: Preserve exponent range in BF16
actual_steps.description: BF16 retains eight exponent bits but only seven fraction bits. It preserves a range similar to FP32 while sacrificing significand precision.

actual_steps.title: Separate storage from arithmetic behavior
actual_steps.description: Both 16-bit formats halve raw value storage relative to FP32. Their different layouts still require appropriate numerical and hardware support.

figures.title: Quantization Engineering Workflow
figures.caption: **Quantization Engineering Workflow**: The tiers order deployment paths by engineering and validation effort, not by format or guaranteed accuracy. PTQ serves as the initial candidate because it operates over frozen weights with zero retraining cost; QAT introduces simulated quantization into the training loop when quality recovery demands backpropagation; specialized sub-4-bit and binary formats require custom kernel execution and extensive hardware-specific validation. Representation choices such as INT8 versus INT4, per-channel scaling, and mixed precision apply across these stages rather than defining separate maturity levels.

figures.title: Calibration Range Selection
figures.caption: **Calibration Range Selection**: Symmetric vs. asymmetric affine quantization mappings. Symmetric quantization (left) forces real zero to map to integer zero, using equal-magnitude negative and positive clipping bounds at the expense of wasted dynamic range for skewed activation distributions; asymmetric quantization (right) uses an explicit zero-point offset $\QuantizationZeroPoint$ to map non-centered ranges $[\ClippingRangeLowerBound, \ClippingRangeUpperBound]$ efficiently.

figures.title: Hardware Specialization Timeline
figures.caption: **Hardware Specialization Timeline**: Computing architectures evolve through recurring cycles of specialization and integration across five eras. Each era introduces domain-specific hardware to resolve an important memory or arithmetic bottleneck, from off-chip FPUs to GPUs, codecs, and TPU/Tensor Core array units. Many of these capabilities later appear alongside CPUs in broader systems, even when the specialized units remain distinct.
figures.alt: Five-column timeline from the 1980s through the 2020s. figures.title: The Rising Ridge
figures.caption: **The Rising Ridge**: Hardware arithmetic intensity (FLOP/byte) over time computed as each chip's dense FP16 tensor peak divided by its memory bandwidth: `{python} RooflineGap.v100_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.v100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for V100, `{python} RooflineGap.a100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.a100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for A100, and `{python} RooflineGap.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` over `{python} RooflineGap.h100_bw_tb_per_s_str` for H100. This is the arithmetic intensity a kernel must reach before compute rather than bandwidth limits it. As compute capability grows faster than memory bandwidth, the ridge point rises from V100 through H100 and remains high on B200. This trend explains why architectures with high data reuse flourish while low-reuse workloads face a growing performance penalty.
figures.alt: Line plot showing dense-FP16 arithmetic intensity ridge points: about 140 FLOP/byte for V100, 153 for A100, 295 for H100, and 281 for B200. Shaded regions indicate memory-rich and compute-dense zones.

figures.title: The Tail Latency Explosion

figures.title: The Throughput-Latency Knee
figures.caption: **The Throughput-Latency Knee**: Batch size vs. throughput (blue) and latency (orange) for the reference ResNet-50 profile on the H100. Throughput rises nearly in proportion to batch size while fixed overhead dominates, then flattens toward its ceiling. Latency grows slowly at first and roughly in proportion to batch size beyond the marked planning knee, where it is twice the batch-one latency and throughput reaches half its ceiling. Each throughput value is batch size divided by the plotted formation-plus-service latency, for a single worker that waits out a 10 ms window and then serves each batch; pipelined serving sustains higher throughput. Values are modeled, not measured.
figures.alt: Dual-axis line chart on a log batch-size axis. Blue line (throughput) rises steeply and then flattens. Orange line (latency) stays nearly flat through batch 32 and then climbs. A vertical dashed line labeled Planning Knee marks batch size near 400.

figures.title: The Business Cost Curve
figures.caption: **The Business Cost Curve**: An equal-class-weighted illustrative cost index vs. classification threshold. Technical metrics like ROC curves hide the economic reality: errors have different costs. Here, a false negative (missed fraud) costs \$500, while a false positive (blocked user) costs \$100. The system flags a transaction as fraud when its score exceeds the threshold, so a lower threshold flags more transactions. Because missing fraud is $5\times$ more costly, the optimal threshold shifts left of center, making the system more aggressive at flagging suspicious transactions and accepting more false positives to minimize expensive misses. With equal costs the optimum would sit at threshold = 0.50; the asymmetry pulls it toward threshold $\approx 0.34$. A population expected cost would also weight each term by class prevalence. MLOps tunes thresholds as costs and prevalence change.
figures.alt: Line chart showing an equal-class-weighted illustrative cost index vs. classification threshold from 0 to 1. Three curves are plotted: false positive cost index (dashed blue) decreasing sigmoidally from left to right, false negative cost index (dashed red) increasing sigmoidally from left to right, and total cost index (solid violet) as their sum forming a U-shape. The optimal threshold is marked with a green dot left of center where the total index is minimized.

figures.caption: **Model Interpretability Spectrum**: A horizontal continuum groups decision trees, linear regression, and logistic regression as intrinsically interpretable, while random forests, neural networks, and CNNs/transformers require post-hoc explanation. It frames an auditability trade-off rather than a universal ranking of model quality.

figures.title: The Cycle of ML Systems (13 Principles)
figures.caption: **The Cycle of ML Systems (13 Principles)**: A four-phase systems engineering lifecycle organized around the conservation-of-complexity heuristic. The phases connect in a feedback cycle, and the thirteen principles sit along the transitions by the part that develops them, spanning bounds, decompositions, fitted models, policy requirements, and design heuristics whose assumptions must be checked. Icons mark the phases: bricks for the data foundations, a neural network for model development, a battery for the efficiency budget of optimization, and a rocket for launch into deployment.

Arrows connect Foundations to Development, Development to Optimization, Optimization to Deployment, and Deployment back to Foundations. The transitions are labeled 1–2 Data as Code and data gravity; 3–4 iron law and Silicon Contract; 5–8 Pareto Frontier, Arithmetic Intensity, Energy-Movement, and Amdahl’s Law; and 9–13 verification gap, Statistical Drift, Skew Diagnostic, Latency Budget, and Bias Feedback. A dashed center circle is labeled Conservation of Complexity.

figures.title: The scale discontinuity
figures.caption: **The scale discontinuity**: On a single machine (left), the usual binding constraint is the memory wall between the accelerators and their high-bandwidth memory, and there are no peers to wait for. In a fleet (right), nodes exchange state over a shared network fabric under a scheduler that places the job and recovers it, so the three C$^3$ roles appear as separate components. The fabric can become the binding network wall, and failed and slow nodes become routine events that hold back the whole job.

One node is marked failed, one is marked slow with a dashed red border, and the other six are labeled waiting. A legend maps dark blue to compute C1, amber to communication C2, and violet to coordination C3.

figures.title: Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps
figures.caption: **Retryable tasks vs. shared training steps**: Map tasks (left) deliver their outputs independently, so a failed task is re-run on its own while the others finish; its missing output delays only the reducers that need it. In synchronous data-parallel training (right), the AllReduce needs every worker's gradient before the shared update can proceed, so a slow worker on the critical path holds the whole step and the healthy workers wait. How much the step stretches depends on overlap and the other costs of the step.
figures.alt: Two timelines with time running left to right. Left, MapReduce: map tasks 1 and 2 run, emit a green output square, and are labeled done; map task 3 runs briefly, is marked failed with a red cross, and then a re-run alone bar on the same lane emits its output, which feeds a reduce bar on the lane below. Right, synchronous training: workers 0 and 1 finish their compute bars early and then show gray wait segments, while worker 2 runs a long red dashed bar labeled slow; all three bars end at an amber AllReduce band, after which an update bar runs on the lane below.

figures.title: Model training compute trends

figures.title: The reliability collapse
figures.caption: **The reliability collapse**: The simultaneous availability of every node required by an unreplicated job, shown as a function of job size for two per-node availability levels under an independence assumption. Even `{python} ReliabilityGap.four_nines_pct_str` per-node availability (green) yields `{python} ReliabilityGap.availability_four_nines_10k_str` at `{python} ReliabilityGap.n_large_str`-node scale.

figures.title: The four infrastructure walls
figures.caption: **The four infrastructure walls**: Read left to right, the examples illustrate four constraints at increasing physical scales; the workload and configuration determine which one binds. The node compares 3.35 TB/s of HBM3 with about 2,000 TFLOP/s of FP8 arithmetic; the four-node DGX H100 rack draws 33.5 kW; the pod compares per-direction NVLink bandwidth with one InfiniBand port, a ninefold budget gap; and the fleet assumes independent GPU failures, reducing a 50,000-hour per-GPU mean time to failure (MTTF) to about 2 hours between failures at 25K GPUs.
figures.alt: An arrow runs from smaller to larger physical scale above four columns. Each column first draws its scale level as parts: a node chassis with 8 GPUs, a rack holding four nodes (32 GPUs), a pod of 32 racks (1,024 GPUs), and a fleet of many pods drawn as plain tiles (10K to 25K GPUs). Below each, a wall panel draws its constraint. Memory wall: a narrow HBM pipe feeds a large FP8 arithmetic block, labeled 3.35 TB/s of HBM feeding about 2,000 TFLOP/s. Power wall: two bars to scale, a traditional rack reaching a gray dashed line labeled 12 kW and a taller DGX H100 bar, labeled 33.5 kW per rack, nearly 3 times a 12 kW rack. Communication wall: a thick NVLink bar above a link one ninth as thick for InfiniBand, labeled 450 to 50 GB/s, a 9 times cliff. Reliability wall: on a log time axis from 1 hour to 10,000 hours, a long gray bar for one GPU and a short red bar for 25K GPUs, labeled MTTF about 2 hours at 25K, from 50,000 hours per GPU.

actual_steps.description: The narrow HBM connection feeds the FP8 arithmetic block. Peak arithmetic is useful only when the workload supplies enough reuse per byte.

actual_steps.title: Cross the node boundary

actual_steps.title: Accumulate failure exposure

figures.title: The accelerator spectrum
figures.caption: **The accelerator spectrum**: Each die is drawn as a grid of 100 cells divided between arithmetic units (dark) and control, cache, and other logic (light), with the medium cells marking the spread of each approximate, illustrative share. Read left to right, the arithmetic share grows from 5 to 10 percent on a CPU to over 90 percent on a custom ASIC, because hardwired dataflow replaces instruction fetch, decode, and scheduling; each step buys throughput per watt by narrowing the range of model architectures the silicon runs well.
figures.alt: Four square dies side by side, CPU, GPU, TPU, and custom ASIC, above an arrow running from general purpose to more specialized. Each die is a 10 by 10 grid of cells: dark cells for arithmetic units, medium cells for the range of estimates, and light cells for control, cache, and other logic. The dark share grows from left to right, labeled 5 to 10 percent for the CPU, 50 to 60 percent for the GPU, 70 to 80 percent for the TPU, and over 90 percent for the custom ASIC. A legend directly under the dies names the three cell types, and the arrow closes the figure below it.

actual_steps.title: Retain general control
actual_steps.description: The CPU reserves most cells for control, caches, and other functions. These support diverse and irregular workloads.

actual_steps.title: Expand parallel arithmetic
actual_steps.description: The GPU allocates a larger share to arithmetic while retaining programmable execution. Its benefit depends on the workload using that parallelism.

actual_steps.title: Match a regular dataflow
actual_steps.description: The TPU panel increases arithmetic share with systolic execution. Nonmatrix work still needs other execution and control resources.

actual_steps.title: Commit to the workload
actual_steps.description: The custom ASIC hardwires more dataflow. Its large arithmetic share trades away flexibility when model operations change.

figures.title: Wafer-scale engine (WSE) architecture
figures.caption: **Wafer-scale engine (WSE) architecture**: A DGX H100 node (left) joins eight separately packaged GPUs through an NVSwitch fabric and must leave the chassis over InfiniBand to reach other nodes, so every exchange crosses a package, board, or network boundary. A WSE (right) instead uses most of a 300 mm wafer as one routed mesh of cores, each with local SRAM; defect-aware routing steers traffic around unusable cores, and the on-wafer mesh replaces off-package transfers for mapped operations. The WSE-3 figures are the vendor's reported totals and are not directly comparable to GPU HBM bandwidth.
figures.alt: Two panels. Left: a DGX H100 node with eight GPU boxes labeled 80 GB, four above and four below a horizontal NVSwitch bar labeled 450 GB/s per GPU each way; an arrow labeled InfiniBand NDR, 50 GB/s per port, leads from the node to a dashed box labeled other nodes. Right: a circular wafer filled with a grid of small core squares joined by mesh links; one core is marked defective with a red X and a highlighted route bends around it. A legend identifies the core, the defective core, and the route, and a note reads WSE-3: 900,000 cores and 44 GB of SRAM, 21 PB/s aggregate SRAM bandwidth.

figures.title: Compute, bandwidth, and power scale at three different rates
figures.caption: **Compute, bandwidth, and power scale at three different rates**: Dense FP16 Tensor throughput, memory bandwidth, and thermal design power for NVIDIA data center accelerators, normalized to the V100 on a log scale, where the shaded gap between the compute and bandwidth lines is the growth in arithmetic intensity a kernel needs to stay compute-bound. Compute rises 18$\times$, bandwidth 8.9$\times$, and TDP 3.3$\times$, so the endpoint gains in arithmetic exceed the gains in memory bandwidth and power allowance. These are peak specifications, not measured application throughput. Specifications come from the MLSysIM hardware registry.
figures.alt: Line chart on a logarithmic growth axis with points placed at their release years, V100 (2017), A100 (2020), H100 (2022), and B200 (2024), so each slope is a growth rate per year. Series are labeled directly at their right ends: dense FP16 Tensor throughput reaching 18 times, memory bandwidth 8.9 times, and dashed thermal design power 3.3 times. The region between the throughput and bandwidth lines is shaded and widens after the A100; a leader into it reads about 2 times FLOP per byte.

figures.title: Tensor Core tiling strategy
figures.caption: **Tensor Core tiling strategy**: Read left to right. To compute one tile of the output matrix $\GemmOutputMatrix$, the kernel streams matching slices of $\GemmLeftOperand$ and $\GemmRightOperand$ from HBM (left) into the SM's shared memory (center), where Tensor Core instructions (right) multiply them many times over while the FP32 partial sums for that $\GemmOutputMatrix$ tile stay in registers. Only after every slice along the shared $\GemmInnerDimension$ dimension has been accumulated is the finished $\GemmOutputMatrix$ tile written back to HBM once, so each byte fetched from HBM feeds many multiply-accumulate operations. The tile shapes shown ($128 \times 32$ slices, a $128 \times 128$ output tile) are one typical choice; kernels tune them to the chip.
figures.alt: Three panels joined by arrows. Left, HBM with full matrices at 3.35 TB/s: matrix A with a row band split into K slices, matrix B with a column band split into K slices, one slice of each dark, and matrix C with one outlined output tile. Center, shared memory with 228 KB per SM: a tall A tile of 128 by 32 and a wide B tile of 32 by 128. Right, Tensor Cores and registers: a grid of small MMA instruction squares above a C tile of 128 by 128 holding FP32 sums. A dashed loop above the panels returns from the Tensor Cores to HBM, labeled repeat per K slice: load the next pair. A solid arrow below returns from the Tensor Cores to C in HBM, labeled after the last slice: write the C tile once.

actual_steps.title: Retain partial sums

figures.title: HBM 3D-stacked architecture
figures.caption: **HBM 3D-stacked architecture**: Left: high-bandwidth memory stacks DRAM dies on a base logic die, links them vertically with through-silicon vias (TSVs), and places the stack on a silicon interposer beside the GPU die, so each stack reaches the GPU over a 1,024-bit interface only millimeters long. Right: DDR5 instead sits on a DIMM across the motherboard, reached over a 64-bit channel through centimeters of board trace. The wider, shorter path raises bandwidth and lowers energy per bit, but HBM bandwidth and capacity remain finite, so the memory wall moves rather than disappears.
figures.alt: Two cross-section panels. Left, HBM stacked beside the die: a GPU die and a stack of eight DRAM dies on a base logic die sit side by side on a silicon interposer above the package substrate, with dashed vertical TSVs through the stack and a thick short link through the interposer labeled 1,024 bits wide, millimeters long. Right, DDR5 across the board: a CPU with its memory controller and a DIMM holding several DRAM chips stand on a motherboard, joined by a thin trace through the board labeled 64 bits wide, centimeters long.

figures.title: Intra-node GPU topology comparison
figures.caption: **Intra-node GPU topology comparison**: Three ways to wire eight GPUs inside one node. Left: a ring gives each GPU only two links, so traffic between distant GPUs passes through up to four hops. Center: a full mesh reaches every peer in one hop but needs $\AcceleratorsPerNode-1$ links per GPU and $\AcceleratorsPerNode(\AcceleratorsPerNode-1)/2$ links in total, which becomes impractical to route beyond about eight GPUs. Right: an NVSwitch fabric gives each GPU one set of links to the switch and puts every pair one switch hop apart, with up to 450 GB/s per direction per H100 SXM GPU (900 GB/s bidirectional); that per-GPU injection bandwidth is not the aggregate bisection bandwidth of the switch fabric.

figures.title: The infrastructure bandwidth hierarchy
figures.caption: **The infrastructure bandwidth hierarchy**: Concentric zones place each tier an ML workload crosses farther from the accelerator's own memory. HBM (3.35 TB/s) sits at the center; the outward tiers are NVLink/NVSwitch (450 GB/s per direction per GPU), one InfiniBand NDR port (50 GB/s per direction), and an illustrative 7 GB/s storage path. Each step outward cuts bandwidth by roughly 7.4, 9, and 7.1 times, not by a universal tenfold law. Exploiting this hierarchy through tiered algorithms is the primary task of distributed systems engineering.

Each tier is named in the top of its band, and its bandwidth is printed on the left radius. On the right radius, dimension arrows span each band and are labeled divide by 7.4, divide by 9, and divide by 7.1. Band widths are proportional to the logarithm of each step, so the InfiniBand band is the widest.

figures.title: The power delivery path
figures.caption: **The power delivery path**: Energy passes through five conversion stages between the medium-voltage grid and the sub-volt supply at the GPU die, and each stage loses a few percent as heat; the band's height is drawn proportional to the power it carries. The per-stage losses shown are illustrative round values, not measurements of a particular facility; compounded, they lose about a fifth of the power, so delivering 1 MW to the dies draws about 1.3 MW before cooling. PUE uses an IT-equipment boundary and includes facility conversion losses as well as cooling; these losses must not be counted twice. The critical engineering challenge is the rack power distribution unit (PDU) to voltage regulator module (VRM) transition, where 10--40 kW of power must be delivered within a single cabinet.
figures.alt: A horizontal band of power flows left to right through five narrow conversion stages: from the utility grid at 13 kV and up, through a transformer to 480 V AC, a UPS at 480 V backup, a rack PDU to 240 V AC, a server PSU to 12 V DC, and a VRM to under 1 V, ending at a dark block labeled GPU dies. The band starts about 1.3 MW tall and ends at 1 MW, and at each stage a thin orange strip peels off downward as heat, labeled about 5, 3, 3, 5, and 8 percent. A dark bracket and a pale tinted region mark the span from the rack PDU through the VRM, labeled inside each cabinet, 10 to 40 kW per rack.

figures.title: Pod-scale network topologies
figures.caption: **Pod-scale network topologies**: Two dominant ways to wire a pod. Left: a switched fat-tree, drawn here as a two-tier leaf and spine fabric in which every leaf switch connects to every spine switch and has as many uplinks as node ports, so any half of the nodes can talk to the other half at full rate (full bisection bandwidth). InfiniBand clusters such as DGX SuperPOD use this design, and larger pods add a third, core tier above the spines. Right: a 2D torus wires each node directly to its four neighbors, and the dashed stubs wrap each row and column around to its opposite edge; bisection bandwidth grows only as $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\ClusterNodeCount})$, so the torus is cheaper at scale but rewards workloads with strong locality, as in Google TPU pods. The choice shapes which parallelism strategies run efficiently.
figures.alt: Two panels. Left, Switched fat-tree: four spine switches in a top row, four leaf switches below with a link from every leaf to every spine, and four nodes under each leaf; leaf L1's four uplinks and four node links are highlighted, and the footer reads L1: 4 uplinks = 4 node ports, full bisection bandwidth. Right, 2D torus: a four-by-four grid of nodes joined to their horizontal and vertical neighbors, with dashed stubs at every row and column end marking wrap-around links; a dashed vertical bisection cut runs down the middle, and the four row links it crosses plus the row wrap-around stubs are highlighted. The footer reads bisection grows as the square root of the node count, each node links to 4 neighbors.

figures.title: The five-level network model for ML training
figures.caption: **The five-level network model for ML training**: Read from the bottom up, each level builds on the one below and becomes more abstract. Level 1 moves bits over wires and optics; Level 2 turns links into reliable, low-overhead transfers between accelerators; Level 3 arranges switches into a topology; Level 4 governs how the fabric behaves under load and congestion; and Level 5 integrates all of them into a production cluster.
figures.alt: Five stacked horizontal bands, labeled L1 at the bottom to L5 at the top, with an upward arrow labeled more abstract. L1, wire and link: PAM4 SerDes, copper DAC, AOC, optics. L2, transport: RDMA, RoCEv2, GPUDirect, alpha-beta cost model. L3, switch and topology: fat-tree, rail-optimized, Dragonfly, torus. L4, fabric behavior: PFC, ECN and DCQCN, incast, adaptive routing. L5, cluster design: pod integration, job placement, failure domains. Beside each band a small schematic shows the level's concrete form: L1, a four-level stepped waveform between two transceivers labeled SerDes; L2, a GPU and its NIC, both labeled, sending to a remote NIC and GPU; L3, two switches linked to all four switches below them; L4, three converging inputs feeding a nearly full queue, with a dashed red arrow labeled PAUSE leaving the queue and pointing back over the inputs; L5, a row of six racks joined by a common bar.

figures.title: From NRZ to PAM4 signaling
figures.caption: **From NRZ to PAM4 signaling**: Both panels send six symbols in the same time over the same total voltage swing. NRZ (left) uses two levels and carries one bit per symbol, 6 bits in all; PAM4 (right) uses four levels and carries two bits per symbol, 12 bits in all, doubling the data rate without raising the symbol rate. The cost is noise margin: adjacent PAM4 levels sit one third as far apart (arrows), so high-speed links need forward error correction (FEC), which adds to the fabric's fixed $\MessageStartupLatency$ latency.
figures.alt: Two waveform panels with six equal symbol slots marked by dashed vertical lines. Left, NRZ: a square wave switching between levels 1 and 0, with one tall shaded band between the two levels and an arrow labeled full swing; below, a strip of six cells holds the bits 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, labeled 6 bits. Right, PAM4: a stepped wave among four levels labeled 00, 01, 10, and 11, with three thin shaded bands between adjacent levels and an arrow labeled one-third swing across one band; below, a strip of twelve cells grouped in pairs holds two bits per symbol, labeled 12 bits.

figures.title: GPUDirect RDMA data path
figures.caption: **GPUDirect RDMA data path**: Without GPUDirect (dashed), a sending node first writes the $\PointToPointMessageSize$-byte payload from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and the NIC then reads it back out, about $2\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes of host-memory traffic per payload. With GPUDirect RDMA (solid), the NIC reads GPU memory directly over the PCIe peer-to-peer path, so the host-memory bounce disappears.
figures.alt: A sending node drawn as its board layout: host memory with a registered buffer and the CPU root complex along the top, a wide PCIe switch in the middle, and GPU memory holding an n-byte payload beside the RDMA NIC along the bottom. A solid green path climbs from GPU memory into the PCIe switch and drops straight down to the NIC, which sends to the fabric. A dashed gray path climbs from GPU memory through the switch to the CPU, then into host memory, labeled 1, write n, and back out, labeled 2, read n, before descending through the switch to the NIC; a note under host memory reads about 2n bytes of bus traffic. A key labels the solid path GPUDirect RDMA and the dashed path staged via host memory.

figures.title: Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA verbs stacks
figures.caption: **Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA verbs stacks**: Read each stack top to bottom through the user-space, kernel, and hardware bands. In the illustrated copied TCP/IP socket path (left), a send enters the kernel through a system call, the payload is copied into kernel socket buffers and again toward the NIC's transmit ring, and the CPU runs the transport protocol in software. With RDMA verbs over InfiniBand or RoCEv2 (right), the collective library posts work requests from user space, the kernel stays off the data path, and the RDMA NIC runs the reliable transport in hardware, reading GPU memory directly through GPUDirect instead of staging a host copy.
figures.alt: Two panels, each divided by dashed lines into user space, kernel, and hardware bands. Left, TCP/IP sockets: training framework in user space, then socket API, TCP/IP stack, and NIC driver in the kernel, then the Ethernet NIC; beside the stack, three payload tiles marked n attach to the framework, the socket API, and the NIC driver and are labeled user buf, socket buf, and TX ring; dashed arrows labeled copy 1 and copy 2 join them, and a thin solid arrow labeled DMA read carries the TX ring into the Ethernet NIC; the footer reads CPU copies data and runs the transport. Right, RDMA verbs: NCCL above the verbs API in user space, then a single amber arrow straight through the empty kernel band, labeled kernel not on the data path, to the RDMA NIC with transport in hardware; a GPU memory box beside the NIC holds a single payload tile and feeds the NIC through a short green arrow; the footer reads NIC reads GPU memory directly (GPUDirect).

figures.alt: Log-log plot of all-reduce time in microseconds from about 10 to 60,000 against message size from 8 bytes to 16 gigabytes. Dotted lines mark the floor and the bandwidth asymptote.

figures.caption: **Non-blocking fat-tree topology**: A three-tier fat-tree built from radix-4 switches ($\SwitchRadix=4$) connects $\SwitchRadix^3/4 = 16$ GPUs through four pods. Leaf and spine switches split their ports equally between the tiers below and above; core switches use all their ports to connect pods. Each tier boundary carries 16 links, supporting full $\BisectionBandwidth$ with suitable routing. The highlighted leaf-spine-core-spine-leaf route between pod 1 and pod 4 is one of $(\SwitchRadix/2)^2 = 4$ equal-cost paths (the other three are drawn lighter), and exploiting those alternatives without excessive reordering requires compatible switch and endpoint mechanisms.

figures.title: Rail-optimized physical wiring
figures.caption: **Rail-optimized physical wiring**: In dense accelerator nodes such as the DGX H100, each GPU's network port is cabled by local slot position: GPU 0 in every node connects to the rail 0 switch, GPU 1 to the rail 1 switch, and so on. Three nodes and four of each node's eight GPUs are drawn, with the rail 0 cables emphasized; further nodes attach to the same rail switches. Tensor-parallel traffic stays on each node's NVSwitch, same-rank data-parallel traffic stays on its own rail, and a spine layer (not drawn) bridges the rails for cross-rank traffic.
figures.alt: A row of four rail switches across the top, each with a short dashed stub upward, the last labeled to spine (not drawn), and a row of three node boxes, Node 0 to Node 2, across the bottom. Each node holds GPU 0 through GPU 3 in a row above a horizontal NVSwitch bar that connects all four. Each GPU has a port on the top edge of its node, and a cable runs from that port up to the switch for its slot: GPU 0 of every node to the rail 0 switch, GPU 1 to rail 1, and so on. The three rail 0 cables and the rail 0 switch are drawn thick and dark; the other cables are thin and light.

figures.title: A PFC deadlock from a cyclic buffer dependency
figures.caption: **A PFC deadlock from a cyclic buffer dependency**: Four switch queues form the cycle of @eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle. Follow the solid arrows clockwise: each full buffer holds packets that need space in the next. The dashed PAUSE frames run counterclockwise, so each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while awaiting space in its downstream successor, and no queue can drain until a watchdog drops packets.
figures.alt: Four switch boxes arranged as a ring, switch 1 at the top, 2 at the right, 3 at the bottom, and 4 at the left, each containing a full red four-slot queue labeled b1 to b4 and the words queue full. Solid dark arrows curve clockwise around the outside of the ring from switch 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 and back to 1, labeled b1 to b2, b2 to b3, b3 to b4, and b4 to b1. Dashed red arrows labeled PAUSE curve counterclockwise around the inside of the ring between the same switches, and the center of the ring reads deadlock.

figures.actual_question: Why can four full queues remain blocked after traffic injection stops?
figures.actual_scope: A directed cycle alone is insufficient: this example additionally assumes occupied buffers, blocked successors, and persistent PAUSE states.

actual_steps.title: Need downstream space
actual_steps.description: Switch 1 holds packets whose next buffer is b2. The solid clockwise arrows continue this requirement through b3 and b4 back to b1.

actual_steps.title: Pause the predecessor
actual_steps.description: Each full queue sends PAUSE upstream, against the forwarding direction. Switch 2 therefore prevents its predecessor from sending more traffic.

actual_steps.title: Close the waiting cycle
actual_steps.description: All four queues wait for successors that are themselves blocked. No queue can drain enough to clear its PAUSE state.

actual_steps.title: Break a dependency
actual_steps.description: In the depicted deadlock, stopping new injection is insufficient. Recovery must break the closed wait, for example through the stated watchdog dropping packets.

figures.title: Parallel file system architecture
figures.caption: **Parallel file system architecture**: A client makes one metadata request (MDS $\to$ MDT) to learn a file's stripe map, then reads the stripes directly from the object storage servers (OSS $\to$ OST) in parallel. Each OST holds every Nth stripe of the file in round-robin order, so consecutive stripes (dark) sit on different servers and one client reads them at once. The shared data path lets every client draw on every OSS, so aggregate bandwidth grows with the number of servers while metadata traffic stays on a separate path.
figures.alt: Architecture diagram with compute clients on the left, a metadata server and a column of object storage servers in the middle, and storage targets on the right. A violet line labeled lookup runs from client 1 to the metadata server, whose target holds a stripe map listing OSTs 1 through N. Green lines join every client through a shared vertical bus to every object storage server. Each object storage target holds stripe tiles of one file: OST 1 holds 0, N, 2N; OST 2 holds 1, N+1, 2N+1; and so on to OST N, with the first tile of each target filled dark green.

figures.title: The data-stall frontier
figures.caption: **The data-stall frontier**: In the ideal overlapped pipeline, the compute active-time fraction is min(1, available bandwidth / input demand), plotted against a logarithmic bandwidth ratio. Markers place three of the chapter's workloads on the curve: the data-stall notebook's pipeline, whose delivery time exceeds its compute window, and the image and text jobs of the text-versus-image bandwidth comparison, each served by the whole parallel file system; arrows from the knee measure each fed job's bandwidth headroom. The curve is an ideal service-rate bound, not an empirical utilization curve or a claim about a storage technology.
figures.alt: Piecewise curve of compute active-time fraction against bandwidth divided by demand on a log axis, rising to one at the matching point, where a knee dot and dashed dropline mark supply equal to demand. A light red band labeled starved shades the region left of the knee and a pale green band labeled fed shades the region to its right. A red marker labeled stalled notebook sits at 0.8 on the rising segment, with a red bar showing the gap up to 1. Green image and text job markers sit on the flat segment, each with an arrow from the knee labeled with its headroom: 3.3 times for the image job and 6,000 times for the text job.

figures.actual_question: When does more input bandwidth stop increasing ideal compute active time?
figures.actual_scope: The curve min(1, bandwidth/demand) is an ideal overlapped service-rate bound. Real utilization can lie below it because of latency, preparation, and coordination.

actual_steps.title: Identify the service deficit
actual_steps.description: Left of matching supply, the input stage cannot deliver batches as fast as compute consumes them. The stalled-notebook point sits at 0.8 ideal active fraction.

actual_steps.title: Reach the knee
actual_steps.description: At bandwidth/demand = 1, input supply matches consumption. The bound reaches active fraction 1 at this service-rate boundary.

actual_steps.title: Interpret moderate headroom
actual_steps.description: The image-job arrow spans 3.3 times matching bandwidth. It is supply margin, not a 3.3-times speedup above full compute activity.

actual_steps.title: Interpret large headroom
actual_steps.description: The text-job arrow spans 6,000 times demand while the bound remains flat. Additional input supply does not accelerate an already fed compute stage in this ideal model.

figures.title: Pipelined data loading
figures.caption: **Pipelined data loading**: Both panels share one time scale, with illustrative stage durations. Sequential loading (a) leaves the GPU idle while each batch is read and prepared. Pipelined loading (b) reads and prepares batch $\BatchIndex+1$ while the GPU trains on batch $\BatchIndex$, so four batches finish in about the time sequential loading needs for two (dashed line). The shaded column marks one instant with three batches in flight. The overlap hides storage latency only while delivery keeps pace with compute and the prefetch buffer is deep enough to absorb variance.

figures.title: Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage path
figures.caption: **Traditional vs. GPUDirect Storage path**: Both panels draw the same node: CPU and host DRAM above a PCIe switch, NVMe and GPU below it. Green routes are DMA transfers of payload bytes. In the buffered path (a), payload climbs into host DRAM and comes back down, and the CPU copies every payload from the kernel buffer to a pinned buffer before the accelerator's DMA can start. In the GDS path (b), NVMe transfers directly into GPU memory, and the dashed CPU link shows the submission and completion work that remains.
figures.alt: Two panels with the same layout: a CPU and a host DRAM box on top, a PCIe switch bar in the middle, and an NVMe SSD and a GPU containing HBM at the bottom. Panel a: a green route labeled DMA 1 runs from the NVMe SSD through the switch up into a kernel buffer in host DRAM; a gray copy arrow joins the kernel buffer to a pinned buffer, with the CPU attached by a link labeled copy; a second green route labeled DMA 2 runs from the pinned buffer down through the switch into HBM. Panel b: one green route labeled DMA runs from the NVMe SSD through the switch into HBM without entering host DRAM, and a dashed gray arrow labeled control runs from the CPU to the NVMe SSD.

figures.title: Two-phase checkpoint staging
figures.caption: **Two-phase checkpoint staging**: Read the lanes left to right. Training pauses only for the local NVMe write ($\TimeInstant_0$ to $\TimeInstant_1$); the copy to the parallel file system overlaps later training steps, and the coordinator publishes the manifest last ($\TimeInstant_3$). Between $\TimeInstant_1$ and $\TimeInstant_3$ the new generation exists only as staged shards, so the previous committed generation remains the restore point.

Brackets below the axis mark the span from t1 to t3 as staged and the span after t3 as restorable.

figures.title: Interconnect bandwidth conventions
figures.caption: **Interconnect bandwidth conventions**: Selected advertised intra-node and inter-node capacities, expressed per direction. NVLink points sum a GPU's links; PCIe uses one x16 interface, and InfiniBand uses one port. These capacities reveal a hierarchy but are not equal-sized endpoint budgets or achieved collective rates. Algorithm selection additionally requires startup cost, port count, routing, and contention. figures.title: Four central collective primitives
figures.caption: **Four central collective primitives**: Standardized patterns for group communication in distributed systems. In each panel the four rows are ranks 0 to 3, read left to right from each rank's input, through the collective, to what each rank holds afterward. (1) AllReduce: all aggregate and all receive the result. (2) AllGather: all send to all and concatenate. (3) ReduceScatter: all aggregate and results are distributed in shards. (4) AllToAll: every process sends unique data to every other process. The two foundational primitives Broadcast (rank 0 sends to all) and Reduce (all aggregate to rank 0) compose the patterns shown here and are defined in the surrounding prose.
figures.alt: Four panels, AllReduce, AllGather, ReduceScatter, and AllToAll, each with rows for ranks 0 to 3. Each row shows the rank's input buffer as small tiles, an amber collective band, and the output buffer. AllReduce: four chunks a to d per rank become four green sums on every rank. AllGather: one chunk per rank becomes four chunks a to d on every rank. ReduceScatter: four chunks per rank become one green sum per rank, sum a on rank 0 through sum d on rank 3. AllToAll: rank i's chunks a_i to d_i are transposed so rank 0 holds a0 to a3, rank 1 holds b0 to b3, and so on. Chunk a has a bold outline in every panel.

figures.title: Ring AllReduce data flow
figures.caption: **Ring AllReduce data flow**: Four GPUs in a logical ring, each gradient split into chunks A to D; the wrap-around link closes the ring from GPU 3 back to GPU 0. (a) After the $\DeviceCount-1$ ReduceScatter steps, in which every GPU sends one chunk to its neighbor and adds the chunk it receives, each GPU holds one fully reduced chunk. (b) After $\DeviceCount-1$ AllGather steps that forward those finished chunks around the same ring, every GPU holds the full sum. Every link carries data in every step, so each GPU sends $2\frac{\DeviceCount-1}{\DeviceCount}\CollectivePayloadSize$ bytes in total, while the $2(\DeviceCount-1)$ steps each pay one startup latency $\MessageStartupLatency$.

Three small tiles ride on each link, naming the chunk that link carries at steps 1, 2, and 3, with fill growing step by step. Row b, after AllGather: every GPU holds all four chunks as green full sums, and the tiles on each link are green.

figures.title: Hierarchical AllReduce
figures.caption: **Hierarchical AllReduce**: Three-phase decomposition that exploits the intra-node/inter-node bandwidth gap. Phase 1 performs intra-node aggregation over NVLink (an NVLink ring acting as a ReduceScatter that leaves each GPU holding a node-shard partial sum), leaving a payload of $\CollectivePayloadSize/\AcceleratorsPerNode$ on each of the $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ GPUs per node. Phase 2 runs an AllReduce across corresponding GPUs using InfiniBand. Phase 3 completes intra-node distribution over NVLink (the AllGather that returns each GPU to the full result). The schematic shows two representative ranks per node; the same decomposition applies to $\AcceleratorsPerNode$ ranks.
figures.alt: Three panels for the three phases, each showing Node 0 above Node 1, each node holding GPU 0 and GPU 1 cards with two shard tiles. Thick NVLink bars join the GPUs inside a node and dashed InfiniBand links join corresponding GPUs across nodes; in each panel only the links in use are amber and the others are light gray. Phase 1, ReduceScatter: NVLink lit, each GPU holds one half-filled node partial sum. Phase 2, Shard AllReduce: InfiniBand lit, one half-filled shard tile rides each inter-node link, and each GPU ends with one green full sum. Phase 3, AllGather: NVLink lit, every GPU holds both green full sums.

figures.title: Dimension-ordered reduction on a torus topology
figures.caption: **Dimension-ordered reduction on a torus topology**: In a 2D torus mesh ($4 \times 4$ node grid representing a simplified TPU pod slice), AllReduce proceeds sequentially along orthogonal dimensions. Phase 1 (orange) executes four parallel horizontal rings across the X dimension ($2(\TorusFirstAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps). Phase 2 (slate) then executes four parallel vertical rings across the Y dimension ($2(\TorusSecondAxisChipCount-1) = 6$ steps) on the row-aggregated partial sums. Dashed stubs mark the torus wrap-around links, each leaving one edge of the grid and re-entering at the opposite edge. This dimension-ordered decomposition needs 12 startup rounds against 30 for a 16-rank 1D global ring, a $2.5\times$ reduction, but each axis processes the full message, so its bandwidth time is $3\CollectivePayloadSize/\LinkBandwidth$ for this grid.

figures.title: Endpoint and in-network reduction
figures.caption: **Endpoint and in-network reduction**: The upstream half of a reduction over four GPUs. (a) Switches only forward packets, so every full gradient tensor crosses the upper links and converges on one reducer GPU, which does all the arithmetic. (b) Aggregation-capable switches add their inputs, so each upper link carries one partial sum and the root switch finishes the reduction; the result then travels back down the same tree. A software reduction tree also aggregates along its path, but performs arithmetic at endpoints rather than switches. The diagram compares where arithmetic happens, not measured speedup.

Panel b: amber switches labeled adds each send one arrow carrying a single half-filled tile g0+g1 or g2+g3 to an amber root switch that adds and holds the green full sum.

figures.title: Communication-computation overlap
figures.caption: **Communication-computation overlap**: The backward pass runs from the last layer to the first, and each layer's gradient AllReduce launches as soon as that layer finishes, so it runs on the network while the GPU computes the next layer's gradients. The first layer finishes last and has no computation left to hide behind, so its AllReduce is exposed before the optimizer step. Overlap succeeds only when the nonoverlappable overhead ($\SymmetricMessageOverhead$) is small, leaving the bulk transfer free to proceed concurrently. Durations are schematic.

figures.title: The memory wall
figures.caption: **The memory wall**: Accelerator memory capacity plotted against the memory a state-of-the-art model needs to train. Training memory assumes 16 bytes per parameter for mixed-precision Adam state; parameter counts are from @epochai2026notable and capacities are vendor specifications.

GPT-3 is circled and annotated as the first plotted model beyond one accelerator, about 35 times the largest of its year. figures.title: The 3D parallelism cube
figures.caption: **The 3D parallelism cube**: The configuration space decomposes cluster training across three orthogonal axes: tensor parallelism ($\TensorParallelDegree$, intra-layer sharding), pipeline parallelism ($\PipelineParallelDegree$, sequential stage partitioning), and data parallelism ($\DataParallelDegree$, batch replication). Each cell is one accelerator, identified by its $(\DataParallelDegree, \PipelineParallelDegree, \TensorParallelDegree)$ coordinate, so the cube holds $\DeviceCount = \DataParallelDegree \times \PipelineParallelDegree \times \TensorParallelDegree$ devices. A feasible point must jointly satisfy model divisibility, per-device memory limits, and the network hierarchy that carries each axis's traffic.

The front bottom right cell is solid navy and marked as one GPU. The cells it communicates with are tinted: the rest of its bottom row is labeled tensor group, the rest of its column is labeled pipeline group, and the cells behind it along the depth are labeled data group. A label reads N equals N DP times N PP times N TP.

figures.title: Data parallelism implementation pipeline
figures.caption: **Data parallelism implementation pipeline**: The five-stage workflow for data-parallel training: (1) partition the global batch, (2) assign sharded mini-batches to individual GPUs, (3) compute independent forward and backward passes to produce local gradients $\MinibatchGradient_i$, (4) execute an AllReduce collective across the cluster to obtain the average gradient $\GlobalBatchGradient$, and (5) update parameters identically across all devices. This strategy preserves the mathematical semantics of single-device SGD while distributing the compute burden.
figures.alt: Five-stage data-parallel workflow across four GPU swimlanes. A green global batch of B equals 128, drawn as sixteen sample tiles in four groups, sends one group of 32 samples to each GPU. Each GPU card holds an identical four-layer model replica and runs forward and backward passes, producing a small signed bar vector g0 to g3 whose bars differ from lane to lane. All four vectors enter one tall amber AllReduce block labeled g global equals one over N times the sum of g i, ring. Every lane then shows the same averaged bar vector g global feeding an update theta card, with the note identical theta on every GPU.

figures.actual_question: Why do independent replicas finish with identical parameter updates?
figures.actual_scope: The diagram describes the shown averaged-gradient SGD workflow; preserving global-batch semantics depends on matching batch and averaging conventions.

actual_steps.title: Partition the global batch
actual_steps.description: The batch of 128 examples becomes four shards of 32 in this illustrated case. Each GPU receives different examples while starting from the same model state.

actual_steps.title: Compute local gradients
actual_steps.description: Each replica performs forward and backward work independently and produces its own gradient gᵢ. Local data differences make those gradients different.

actual_steps.title: Average across replicas
actual_steps.description: AllReduce combines all local gradients into one global average. This collective synchronizes the update information, rather than sending examples through the GPUs in sequence.

actual_steps.title: Apply the same update
actual_steps.description: Every GPU applies the common averaged gradient and reaches the same updated parameters. Replica agreement is what permits the next global-batch step.

figures.title: Communication patterns and their costs
figures.caption: **Communication patterns and their costs**: Ring AllReduce and a parameter server illustrate two ways to aggregate updates. All-to-All instead routes distinct data to each peer; the complete graph shows logical destinations, not a requirement for dedicated physical links. A switched fabric can carry this traffic, with cost determined by message size, routes, and contention.
figures.alt: Three panels. Ring AllReduce: four GPUs, each holding its gradient as four chunk cells, pass one numbered chunk to the next neighbor around a ring, with equal-weight arrows on every link, labeled 2 times N minus 1 over N times M per GPU, load spread over all links. Parameter server: four workers exchange data with a shared bus that feeds one thick red trunk into a highlighted red server NIC beneath the server, labeled 2M per worker, all traffic through one NIC. Logical All-to-All: four GPUs with four chunk cells each, joined by twelve directed arrows, one per ordered pair, labeled N times N minus 1 messages, logical pairs rather than physical wires.

figures.title: Distributed synchronization models
figures.caption: **Distributed synchronization models**: The timelines compare three synchronization strategies. Top: bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) forces all workers to wait at a global barrier every step. Middle: stale synchronous parallel (SSP) allows workers to proceed up to $\StalenessBound$ steps ahead of the slowest worker. Bottom: asynchronous parallel (ASP) execution removes the global update barrier while allowing gradient staleness; communication and resource contention can still delay progress.
figures.alt: Timeline diagram with three panels of four worker rows, in which worker W3 takes longer per iteration than the others. Top, BSP: after every iteration the faster workers sit in red-hatched wait blocks until W3, labeled slow in red, reaches a global barrier. Middle, SSP with s equal to 1: the faster workers run freely until they would lead W3 by more than one iteration, then pause briefly. Bottom, ASP: every worker runs without waiting, so the faster workers finish eight iterations while W3 finishes six.

figures.actual_question: What does relaxing a global barrier permit workers to do?
figures.actual_scope: The timelines are schematic; removing a global barrier does not eliminate resource contention or guarantee better convergence.

actual_steps.title: Wait at every barrier
actual_steps.description: BSP holds workers at each step boundary until the slow worker arrives. Hatched waits accumulate even on workers that finished their compute.

actual_steps.title: Permit a bounded lead
actual_steps.description: SSP allows workers to move ahead only within its staleness bound. Faster workers eventually wait when that allowance is exhausted.

actual_steps.title: Remove the global barrier
actual_steps.description: ASP lets workers advance without a global update barrier. Their progress diverges, so updates may use stale state; communication and contention still impose delays.

figures.title: ZeRO memory reduction
figures.caption: **ZeRO memory reduction**: Standard data parallelism (DDP) replicates all model states across every GPU. ZeRO progressively partitions these states: ZeRO-1 shards optimizer states, ZeRO-2 adds gradient sharding, and ZeRO-3 shards the parameters themselves; each dashed outline marks the replicated stack a stage no longer holds. ZeRO-3 achieves linear memory scaling, enabling models with 100B+ parameters to fit on accelerators that could not hold the replicated state.
figures.alt: Stacked bar chart of per-GPU memory for optimizer state, gradients, and weights, shaded from darker to lighter blue, under DDP, ZeRO-1, ZeRO-2, and ZeRO-3. Totals fall from 112 GB to 29.3, 15.5, and 1.75 GB; a red dashed line at 80 GB accelerator memory, with the region above it washed light red, shows that only DDP exceeds it. Behind each ZeRO bar a dashed gray outline at the 112 GB DDP height marks the replicated state that stage no longer holds on the GPU.

figures.title: The scaling tax
figures.caption: **The scaling tax**: Effective speedup $\DeviceCount/(1+(\DeviceCount-1)\SerialFraction)$ against GPU count on log-log axes, for illustrative fixed residual fractions $\SerialFraction$ of baseline step time. figures.title: Matrix partitioning under tensor parallelism
figures.caption: **Matrix partitioning under tensor parallelism**: A Megatron-LM layer pair on two GPUs, read left to right. The first layer (for example, QKV or the first feed-forward layer) is split by columns, $\ColumnParallelWeightMatrix = [\ColumnParallelWeightMatrix_1 \mid \ColumnParallelWeightMatrix_2]$, so each GPU computes its own slice $\LayerOutputMatrix_i$ of the replicated input's output. The second layer is split by rows, $\RowParallelWeightMatrix = [\RowParallelWeightMatrix_1 ; \RowParallelWeightMatrix_2]$, so each slice feeds its matching shard on the same GPU without communication. The only collective is the amber AllReduce that sums the partial outputs $\RowParallelOutputMatrix_1 + \RowParallelOutputMatrix_2$, leaving the full result on both GPUs.
figures.alt: Two GPU lanes, each written as a matrix equation with rectangles drawn to shape. On each lane a replicated input matrix X multiplies weight matrix A, of which the GPU holds only one column half, A1 or A2, the other half dashed. The result is one column slice, Y1 or Y2, which multiplies the matching row half of B, B1 on top for GPU 0 and B2 below for GPU 1, giving a full-size partial sum Z1 or Z2; a note between the lanes reads no communication. Both partial sums enter one amber AllReduce bar spanning the lanes, which outputs the full Z on each GPU.

figures.title: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) AllToAll routing
figures.caption: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) AllToAll routing**: Expert parallelism on four ranks, one expert per rank, read left to right and drawn for top-1 routing with one token traced. Each rank's gate picks the top-$\RoutedExpertCount$ experts for its tokens; the first All-to-All dispatches every token to the rank that hosts its expert, the experts compute, and a second All-to-All returns the results so each rank can form the gate-weighted sum for its own tokens. In both exchanges every rank may send to every other rank, which is why the pattern stresses the fabric's bisection bandwidth.
figures.alt: Five columns over four rows. On the left, ranks 0 to 3 each hold four token chips lettered a to p. An amber dispatch band carries one line per token to the blue expert box on the rank its gate chose, so Expert 0 holds tokens b, g, i, p, Expert 1 holds d, e, k, n, Expert 2 holds a, h, j, o, and Expert 3 holds c, f, l, m, one token from every rank. A second amber return band carries each token back to its home rank, where the four chips reappear in their original order shaded blue. The route of token a, from rank 0 to Expert 2 and back, is drawn heavier.

figures.title: Parallelism strategy decision framework
figures.caption: **Parallelism strategy decision framework**: A selection guide that begins with memory fit. For a model that fits on one device, evaluate data parallelism against the throughput target and input-delivery budget; the complete dataset need not fit in accelerator memory. A model that does not fit is routed by the structure that breaks the budget, with sequential depth leading to pipeline parallelism, an oversized single layer to tensor parallelism, and otherwise sharded data parallelism (FSDP/ZeRO). Combine parallelism axes when the workload requires them. Peak memory, global batch, bandwidth, and workload imbalance constrain every candidate.
figures.alt: Decision tree flowchart. From the workload profile, diamonds ask whether the model fits on one GPU, whether one GPU meets the target, whether the layer stack is deep, and whether a single layer is too large. Outcomes are single device, data parallel, pipeline parallel, tensor parallel, or sharded data parallel (FSDP, ZeRO), each with a small glyph of layer bars inside GPU frames: one full stack for a single device, three full copies for data parallel, two frames holding upper and lower layer groups for pipeline parallel, two frames each holding one half of every layer for tensor parallel, and three frames each holding a different one-third slice of every layer, the rest dashed, for sharded data parallel. Dashed lines from the four parallel outcomes lead to a box that combines axes as TP times PP times DP.

figures.title: Fail-stop vs. Byzantine failures
figures.caption: **Fail-stop vs. Byzantine failures**: In the fail-stop model (left), a failed worker simply ceases to send messages, which a timeout flags as suspect without distinguishing a crash from delay or isolation. In the Byzantine model (right), a failed worker continues to participate but sends incorrect data (for example, corrupted gradients reported as valid), which can poison the global model state if not detected by redundant validation.
figures.alt: Two panels divided by a dashed line, each showing four worker message streams along a time axis with a liveness column at the right. Caption text reads silence is the evidence. Right, Byzantine: W5 to W8 send amber gradient squares on the same schedule and all four get green checks, but partway along W6's row its squares turn red. Text reads on time, but wrong.

figures.title: Hierarchy of failure domains
figures.caption: **Hierarchy of failure domains**: Failure domains are often nested or overlapping. A GPU failure affects one device. figures.title: The bathtub curve
figures.caption: **The bathtub curve**: Hardware failure rates $\ComponentHazardRate(\TimeInstant)$ vary over time. (1) Infant mortality: high failure rate initially due to manufacturing defects. (2) Useful life: constant, low failure rate where random failures dominate. (3) Wear-out: increasing failure rate as components age. Burn-in testing aims to filter out infant mortality failures before deployment.
figures.alt: Line graph of failure rate versus component age from days to end of life, showing a bathtub shape across three shaded regions separated by dashed lines: (1) infant mortality in red with a falling rate from manufacturing defects screened by burn-in, (2) useful life in green with a constant rate whose flat floor is highlighted and labeled h equals 1 over MTTF, with MTTF about 50,000 hours, and (3) wear-out in red with a rising rate from electromigration and thermal fatigue.

figures.title: The ML failure spectrum
figures.caption: **The ML failure spectrum**: Hardware faults ordered by how long they persist. A transient fault leaves nothing to repair, an intermittent fault returns under the load that exposed it, and a permanent fault repeats on every retry. Persistence decides the fleet response, from retry through quarantine to replacement, and fault tolerance engineering must handle all three to keep a fleet making progress.

figures.title: Hot-spare failover
figures.caption: **Hot-spare failover**: An $\DeviceCount+1$ pool of four active GPUs and one standby spare. When loss or gradient sanity checks flag a suspect GPU and replay implicates it, the job drains that device and resumes on the spare from the last known-good state; the device goes to repair and a healthy unit refills the spare slot. Google's data-center examples use this reactive pattern to keep training moving despite hardware faults, in contrast to running every computation on two or three redundant units and comparing results [@dean2024mlsys]. The standing cost is the idle spare.
