figures.title: Error masking
figures.caption: **Error masking**: Follow a soft error from the top. It becomes a failure only if the corrupted data is read and then also produces incorrect output; at each No branch it is masked, first by microarchitectural effects (unused components, overwritten values, squashed speculative instructions) and then by software effects (dead instructions, logical and compare operations, uninfluential branches). Because software-level fault injection sees only the second filter, it can misestimate a system's true resilience to transient errors.
figures.alt: Flowchart starting at a soft error. A decision diamond asks whether corrupted data is read; No leads to masked in the microarchitecture. Yes leads to a second diamond asking whether output is incorrect or the system crashes; No leads to masked in software, Yes leads to failure. Beside each masked outcome, three masking causes are listed: unused component, overwritten value, and squashed speculation for the microarchitecture; dead instruction, logical or compare op, and uninfluential branch for software. The failure path, Yes and then Yes from soft error to failure, is drawn as a heavy red spine; the No exits are thin gray arrows. A dashed arrow labeled software fault injection enters the spine after the first diamond, and a shaded region below that point, labeled view of software fault injection, encloses only the second diamond, its masked exit, and the failure.

figures.title: The checkpoint trade-off
figures.caption: **The checkpoint trade-off**: Checkpoint save overhead (dashed blue) falls as the interval lengthens, while expected rework after a failure (dashed red) rises; their sum (solid) is minimized at the Young-Daly interval. The curves use this chapter's 175B running example on its `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.n_gpus_str`-GPU cluster, with a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.t_write_s_str` checkpoint write and a `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.mtbf_h_str` full-system MTBF, which put the optimum near `{python} CheckpointTradeoffInputs.tau_opt_min_str`. The minimum is shallow, so an interval somewhat off the optimum costs little, while a far shorter or far longer one costs a great deal.

A dotted dropline from the minimum passes through an open circle where the two dashed terms cross, labeled terms equal. The background left of the optimum is tinted blue and labeled writes dominate; the background to the right is tinted red and labeled rework dominates. Each curve carries a direct label.

figures.title: Checkpoint-recovery timeline
figures.caption: **Checkpoint-recovery timeline**: A training run alternates productive compute (blue) with durable checkpoint writes (green). When a failure strikes, all compute since the last completed checkpoint is lost (red hatching), and the job must then read the checkpoint and restart (red) before productive compute resumes. A failure therefore costs the rework since the last save plus the recovery latency; the Young-Daly interval trades the first of these against the write time paid at every checkpoint.

Bottom, a progress line on the same time axis rises during compute and stays flat during each save, with green dots marking durable progress at the end of each save. During the lost block the line rises in red, then at the failure a red dashed arrow drops it back to the last durable level, it stays flat through recovery, and it climbs again.

figures.title: Distributed checkpoint architecture
figures.caption: **Distributed checkpoint architecture**: Centralized vs. sharded checkpoint writes. In the centralized pattern (left), every worker funnels its shard through one coordinator, whose ingress bandwidth and buffering constrain the write path and whose failure halts the save. In the distributed pattern (right), each worker writes its own shard to local NVMe in parallel and a background process drains the shards to remote object storage, so the local blocking write time can remain roughly constant with fixed shard sizes and sufficient staging bandwidth; shared drain capacity still limits completion.
figures.alt: Two panels divided by a dashed line. Left, centralized: four workers send red arrows that merge into one coordinator box labeled ingress limit, which writes to shared storage; beneath, a timing strip shows the four workers' green shard writes in a staircase, one after another, with a red bracket reading blocking write grows with workers. Right, distributed: each of four workers writes with a green arrow to its own NVMe drive, and dashed arrows drain the drives to an object store labeled background; beneath, the four green shard writes start together and end together under a green bracket labeled blocking, followed by dashed gray bars under a bracket labeled drain in background.

figures.title: Elastic training recovery
figures.caption: **Elastic training recovery**: Read the three phases top to bottom. Rather than restoring the original worker count before resuming, elastic training pauses when a node fails, reloads the last consistent checkpoint, re-forms the ring over the $\DeviceCount-1$ survivors, and redistributes the failed node's data shards among them. The job resumes at reduced throughput (75 percent here, assuming an unchanged per-worker rate), turning a hard failure into a temporary slowdown.

figures.title: The three pillars of observability
figures.caption: **The three pillars of observability**: Diagnosis of fleet failures can combine three signal types. Metrics reveal *when* and *where* a problem occurs (for example, GPU utilization drops). Logs provide the *what* through event context (for example, an out-of-memory exception). Traces expose the *request path* by linking events across the distributed lifecycle (for example, identifying the request that triggered the memory spike). A single signal can justify immediate mitigation; joining signals on shared identifiers strengthens diagnosis without proving the cause.
figures.alt: Three panels draw each signal in its native form. Metrics, labeled when and where: a GPU utilization time series that runs level and then drops sharply in red. Logs, labeled what happened: a stream of gray log lines with one red monospace line reading OOM exception. Traces, labeled request path: a waterfall of nested span bars with one long span outlined in red. In each panel a dashed violet connector leaves the red anomaly, the end of the utilization drop, the end of the OOM line, and the end of the red span, and runs down as an arrow into a bar reading correlate on shared identifiers, listing request, trace, model version, feature version, and deployment, which leads to a recovery action box: shed load, restart, roll back, or degrade.

figures.actual_scope: Correlated observations narrow causes; correlation by itself does not prove a physical or software root cause.

actual_steps.description: Request, trace, model, feature, and deployment identifiers connect events belonging to the same operating context. An unrelated log message is weaker evidence.

figures.title: Training failure signatures
figures.caption: **Training failure signatures**: Common patterns of model loss over time that indicate underlying system or algorithmic failures. (A) Normal training. (B) Gradient explosion. (C) Loss plateau. (D) NaN divergence, ending where a nonfinite-value check halts the run; without such a check the process can keep running on NaN values rather than crash. Identifying these signatures automatically is essential for rapid recovery in autonomous training pipelines. The curves are synthetic illustrations of each pattern, not logs from a training run.
figures.alt: Four loss-versus-steps panels in a two-by-two grid on a shared loss axis. (A) Normal training: a green curve descending smoothly. Panels B to D repeat that healthy curve as a faint green reference line behind each pathology. (B) Gradient explosion: a descending curve with a red spike segment midway that then rejoins the healthy reference, labeled healthy. (C) Loss plateau: a curve that flattens early, with the gap between it and the healthy reference shaded red and labeled gap to healthy. (D) NaN divergence: a curve that pulls away above the healthy reference, oscillating with growing amplitude, then climbs steeply to a red X labeled NaN check halts run.

figures.title: Scheduling trade-offs across competing fleet objectives
figures.caption: **Scheduling trade-offs across competing fleet objectives**: A four-way trade-off diamond (Throughput, Latency, Fairness, Cost Efficiency) illustrates the tensions governing cluster scheduling. Throughput favors long, unbroken runs; Latency favors aggressive preemption for interactive jobs; Resource-share fairness can constrain placement to equalize shares; and Cost Efficiency uses discounted, interruptible capacity. Each vertex sketches a four-GPU pool over time as that objective would schedule it and names a possible cost of favoring it; the conflicts depend on workload and available capacity.
figures.alt: Four violet-outlined cards arranged as a diamond and joined by dashed edges, each holding a small strip of a four-GPU pool against time, with strip height standing for GPUs, and a line naming what that objective gives up. Throughput, at top: one large gang block runs unbroken across the whole strip while three small jobs wait stacked in a dashed queue column to its left; gives up small jobs, which starve. Cost efficiency, at left: three spot blocks separated by two red preemption ticks, each tick followed by a red hatched stretch of redone work; gives up preemption overhead. Fairness, at right: team A holds half the pool for the whole period, team B holds the other half briefly and the rest of its share sits idle with a dashed outline; gives up peak utilization. Latency, at bottom: the gang block is cut by two red preemption ticks so short gray jobs can start, leaving the gang in fragments; gives up large gangs, which fragment. The center reads a scheduling policy sets the weights.

figures.title: The distributed deadlock (hold and wait)
figures.caption: **The distributed deadlock (hold and wait)**: In a non-gang scheduler (left), job J1 acquires half the cluster and waits for the rest, while job J2 acquires the other half and waits for J1 to release its GPUs. Neither can proceed, and 100 percent of the cluster sits idle. Gang scheduling (right) solves this by mandating atomic allocation: a job is either granted its entire $\DeviceCount$-GPU requirement simultaneously or it waits in the queue without holding any resources.
figures.alt: Two panels, each with a queue lane above eight GPU rows against a time axis. Left, partial allocation: J1 holds GPU rows 0 to 3 and J2 holds rows 4 to 7, both drawn as red hatched blocks labeled holds 4 of 8 that extend past the right edge with dashed ends; two curved red arrows form a cycle between them labeled waits, and the panel reads 8 GPUs held, none computing. Right, gang scheduling: a blue J1 block spans all eight rows, then a blue J2 block spans all eight rows after it, each labeled all 8 at once; above them, J2 waits in the queue in a dashed violet box labeled holds 0 until an arrow labeled J1 finishes drops it into the GPUs. The panel reads no partial holds, no deadlock.

figures.title: Architectural paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes
figures.caption: **Architectural paradigms: Slurm vs. Kubernetes**: Slurm (left) uses an imperative batch model where users submit explicit resource requests to a centralized controller (`slurmctld`) providing deterministic atomic allocation. Kubernetes (right) uses a declarative service model where controllers continuously reconcile observed cluster state in `etcd` against desired state specifications.
figures.alt: Two columns. Left, Slurm, drawn as a straight one-way line: a job script with an sbatch command flows down once to slurmctld, then to slurmd on each node, whose connectors end on one dashed violet outline enclosing four nodes; the note reads all nodes granted at once, or the job waits. Right, Kubernetes, drawn as a closed loop: a desired-state file applied with kubectl flows into the API server and etcd, which holds two slots reading desired 4 pods and observed 3. Three violet arrows then form a cycle labeled reconcile loop: watch, from etcd down to the controllers, which act on the gap; recreate, from the controllers to a group of four pods, of which Pod 3 is drawn red and dashed and labeled failed; and status, from the pods back up into etcd. The note reads observed state is reconciled continuously.

figures.caption: **Hierarchical placement for 3D parallelism**: This placement example maps distributed training dimensions to physical interconnect layers. figures.title: Elastic training worker lifecycle and state machine
figures.caption: **Elastic training worker lifecycle and state machine**: The state machine governing dynamic worker membership. Active training loops on step completion and leaves that state along three paths: idle GPUs trigger scale up, a preemption for higher-priority work triggers scale down, and a host timeout or ECC error triggers worker replacement. Each path rebuilds the communication group and returns to active training (dashed arrows), and a spot reclamation deadline can force a shrinking job straight into replacement. Worker processes may restart during resizing, so recovery requires the application to restore valid training state.
figures.alt: State machine with a central active training state that has a step completion self-loop. Solid arrows lead from it to scale up on idle GPUs, to scale down on preemption, and to replace worker on host timeout or ECC error. Dashed arrows return to active training labeled group rebuilt, ranks released, and spare joined. A red dashed arrow labeled spot reclaim deadline runs from scale down to replace worker.

figures.title: Capacity reservation tiers and portfolio optimization
figures.caption: **Capacity reservation tiers and portfolio optimization**: This constructed portfolio combines reserved physical capacity, on-demand acquisitions, and interruptible workers. Reserved capacity covers the steady 60 percent base, on-demand the next 20 percent, and spot the peak; these shares and the demand curve are scenario assumptions. A discount commitment alone does not reserve capacity, and on-demand admission is not instantaneous. Schedulers map steady-state baseline demand to reserved capacity, diurnal spikes to on-demand instances, and restart-tolerant training to discounted spot pools. figures.title: Iron law diagnostic flowchart
figures.caption: **Iron law diagnostic flowchart**: A troubleshooting flow that starts from a missed step-time or token-latency target and low accelerator utilization, branches through I/O, CPU, and communication-overhead checks, and classifies the workload as compute-bound or memory-bound at the leaves. Compute-bound paths point to lower-precision arithmetic and to reductions in active work such as MoE routing, whose saving becomes weight bytes rather than arithmetic in batch-one decode (@sec-performance-engineering-moe); memory-bound paths point to operator fusion, tiling, weight quantization, and speculative decoding. Overhead-bound symptoms (data loading, preprocessing, communication) are surfaced earlier in the flow and addressed before the final compute/memory classification.
figures.alt: Troubleshooting flowchart starting from a box reading Target is missed. A GPU-utilization check sends its yes branch right along an overhead lane: an I/O-bound check whose yes branch leads to a green More DL workers box, then a CPU-bound check whose yes branch leads to a green Offload preprocessing box, and whose no branch ends at a violet Comm overhead box. The utilization check's no branch leads down into a panel titled Intensity greater than ridge, which draws a small roofline: a blue rising slope over a blue memory-bound region meets a flat orange ceiling over an orange compute-bound region at a dot marked ridge. Below the blue region, a blue group holds operator fusion and INT4 or speculative decoding; below the orange region, an orange group holds FP8 math and MoE routing. Every remedy joins a bus into a Re-profile workload box, and a dashed loop labeled iterate until the target is met returns to the start.

actual_steps.title: Start outside the kernel
actual_steps.description: A missed target with low accelerator utilization first calls for stall diagnosis. An accelerator waiting for input cannot benefit from faster arithmetic alone.

actual_steps.title: Eliminate feeding overhead
actual_steps.description: The right branch checks I/O, CPU preprocessing, and exposed communication. Each branch names a different intervention because each delays useful device work differently.

actual_steps.title: Classify busy execution
actual_steps.description: Once the device is usefully occupied, compare arithmetic intensity with the ridge point. Below the ridge the bandwidth bound is tighter; above it the compute bound is tighter.

actual_steps.title: Choose and verify a remedy
actual_steps.description: Memory-bound remedies reduce traffic or improve reuse; compute-bound remedies reduce arithmetic cost or active work. Re-profile because removing one bottleneck can expose another.

figures.title: FlashAttention memory hierarchy tiling
figures.caption: **FlashAttention memory hierarchy tiling**: Block-by-block scheduling of Q, K, and V matrices loaded into on-chip shared memory (SRAM). Attention scores are computed and rescaled online without materializing the quadratic $\SequenceLength \times \SequenceLength$ intermediate matrix in off-chip HBM, keeping persistent attention workspace linear in sequence length for fixed head dimension. HBM traffic still depends on SRAM capacity and tile reloads.
figures.alt: Two side-by-side regions. The left HBM region, labeled 3.35 TB/s, draws the attention operands as strips around a six-by-six grid: Q as a vertical strip of row blocks on the left, K transpose as a horizontal strip of column blocks above, V as a strip of blocks below, and O as a vertical strip on the right. The grid is the S by S score matrix, drawn with dashed red lines and labeled never written, 134 MB per head at S = 8,192. Block Q i, block K j, and block V j are filled dark blue; in grid row i, two tiles are shaded gray as already processed, tile S i j is orange, and an orange arrow runs along the rest of the row; block O i is green. A blue arrow labeled load Q i, K j, V j enters the right SRAM region, labeled on chip, about 228 KB per SM, which holds the three dark blue tiles feeding an orange score tile, S i j equals Q i K j transpose, then an online softmax box with running max and sum, then a green accumulate O i box that V j also feeds. A green arrow labeled write O i returns to HBM.

figures.title: Block-wise versus per-tensor quantization
figures.caption: **Block-wise versus per-tensor quantization**: Under per-tensor scaling (left), one outlier weight sets the scale for the whole tensor, so six of the seven small weights round to zero and the seventh rounds to one. Under block-wise quantization (right), each group of weights gets its own scale: the block without the outlier keeps full INT8 resolution, while the small weights that share the outlier's block are still crushed. Smaller blocks confine the damage further at the cost of more scale metadata.
figures.alt: Two side-by-side panels quantize the same eight FP16 weights, one of which is an outlier of 58.7. Left, per-tensor: a single scale of about 0.462 maps six weights to 0, one to 1, and the outlier to 127, with the collapsed cells shaded red. Right, block-wise with blocks of four outlined by dashed boxes: the first block's scale of about 0.00165 maps its weights to 73, -48, 127, and -91, shaded green, while the second block, containing the outlier, maps to 127, 0, 1, and 0.

figures.title: Deep learning compilation pipeline
figures.caption: **Deep learning compilation pipeline**: The four-stage lowering flow from eager Python bytecode through graph capture (TorchDynamo), graph-level optimization (AOTAutograd decomposition and FX passes), target-aware operator fusion (TorchInductor), and code generation with autotuned GPU kernels (Triton and cuBLAS). Each column traces the same feed-forward block: bias additions fold into the GEMMs, GELU fuses into the first GEMM as an epilogue, and four captured operations lower to three kernels. Orange marks the compute-heavy GEMMs and blue the element-wise and normalization operations whose cost is memory traffic, so fusion folds a blue operation into an orange kernel as its epilogue.
figures.alt: Four numbered stage headings across the top: graph capture with TorchDynamo, graph optimization with AOTAutograd and FX passes, operator fusion with TorchInductor, and code generation with Triton and cuBLAS. Below each heading, a vertical chain traces one feed-forward block on four aligned rows, with dotted lines linking each operation to its counterpart in the next stage. GEMM and Linear boxes are orange; GELU and LayerNorm boxes are blue. Stage 1 shows Linear, GELU, Linear, LayerNorm. Stage 2 shows GEMM plus bias, GELU, GEMM plus bias, LayerNorm. Stage 3 encloses the first GEMM plus bias and GELU in a dashed group. Stage 4 shows three kernels: one tall orange GEMM plus GELU kernel with a blue fused epilogue band inside it, into which both upper rows converge, then GEMM with cuBLAS and LayerNorm as a Triton kernel. Counts under the columns read 4 ops, 4 ops, 3 groups, and 3 kernels.

figures.title: End-to-end inference pipeline
figures.caption: **End-to-end inference pipeline**: One language-model request crosses between CPU and GPU twice. The load balancer routes and admits it and the CPU tokenizes it; prefill then processes the whole prompt in one pass and writes its keys and values to the KV cache, and decode reads and appends that cache one token per step before the CPU detokenizes the stream. The strip orders one request's latency, with illustrative segment widths. Everything up to the end of prefill counts against time to first token, and the routing and CPU segments are serving-tax work that spends latency budget outside GPU compute.
figures.alt: Two regions labeled CPU and GPU. In the CPU region, requests flow down through a load balancer and a tokenizer. Token IDs pass right to a prefill box in the GPU region, which writes to a KV cache box. A decode box reads from and appends to the KV cache, loops on itself, and sends generated token IDs left to a detokenize box that feeds a response stream. Below, a horizontal strip divides one request's latency into route, pre, prefill, decode steps, and post segments, the decode segment ticked into per-token steps, with brackets marking time to first token and TPOT times output tokens.

figures.title: Batching strategies compared
figures.caption: **Batching strategies compared**: Four requests of different lengths arrive one time unit apart under three policies; the timings are illustrative. (a) Without batching, each request receives its own forward pass, so later arrivals queue behind earlier ones and the GPU runs four passes. (b) Static batching holds every request until the batch of four is full, then runs one pass padded to the longest request; early arrivals pay the longest wait. (c) Dynamic batching dispatches whatever has arrived when a short window closes, limiting intentional formation delay in this timeline while sharing each pass between two requests. Waiting for an occupied worker remains a separate source of delay.
figures.alt: Three stacked timelines labeled (a) no batching, (b) static batching, and (c) dynamic batching. Each shows four request rows R1 to R4 with arrival ticks, gray wait segments, blue forward-pass segments, and hatched padding, above a GPU row. The GPU row shows four single-request passes in (a), one four-request pass in (b), and two two-request passes in (c). Dashed violet lines mark when each batch is dispatched.

figures.title: Static vs. continuous batching
figures.caption: **Static vs. continuous batching**: In static batching (a), completed slots cannot be reused until the longest request finishes, although completed responses may already be released. Continuous batching (b) admits waiting requests into freed slots at iteration boundaries, starting each with a prefill step. Over the eight iterations shown, 20 of 32 slot-iterations do useful work under static batching and all 32 under continuous batching; the hatched idle slots are the capacity recovered when arrivals and cache capacity permit.
figures.alt: Two stacked grids of four slots by eight iterations. Bottom: continuous batching, where requests R5, R6, and R7 enter the freed slots with a dark prefill cell and continue decoding, leaving no idle cells; a note reads 32 of 32 slots busy. Final-token cells are green.

figures.caption: **The KV cache wall**: Total GPU memory usage for a 4-bit quantized 70B model (`{python} KVCacheWallInputs.weights_gb_str` weights) on an `{python} KVCacheWallInputs.hbm_gb_str` H100. figures.title: KV cache fragmentation and the PagedAttention solution
figures.caption: **KV cache fragmentation and the PagedAttention solution**: The panels replay the eight-slot example from the text. (a) Contiguous reservation holds the maximum length of four slots per sequence, so the slots Seq A and Seq B never fill sit idle (internal fragmentation). (b) After sequences finish, four slots are free but the largest contiguous gap is two, so Seq E, which needs four contiguous slots, cannot be admitted (external fragmentation). (c) PagedAttention maps Seq E's logical pages through a block table onto any free physical blocks, so the same memory now holds it; only the unfilled tail of its final block remains unused.
figures.alt: Three panels built from eight memory slots. Panel a: Seq A uses two of its four reserved slots and Seq B uses three of four; the unused reserved slots are hatched. Panel b: slots 2 and 3 hold Seq C and slots 6 and 7 hold Seq D, leaving two 2-slot gaps; four dashed red cells for Seq E, which needs four contiguous slots, do not fit. Panel c: Seq E's logical pages 0 to 3 pass through a block table mapping them to physical slots 0, 1, 4 and 5 among the C and D slots; page 3's slot is only partly filled. A legend identifies in-use entries, reserved but unused slots, free slots and other sequences.

figures.title: Prefix caching via block sharing
figures.caption: **Prefix caching via block sharing**: PagedAttention enables efficient prefix caching by allowing multiple sequences' block tables to point to the same physical blocks for shared content. In this example, the System Prompt is stored in blocks 0-5. Request A and Request B map their first 6 logical pages to these same physical blocks, storing only their unique suffixes in new blocks. This dramatically reduces memory usage and prefill computation for workloads with shared context.

Request A's gray suffix pages P6 and P7 point to private blocks B10 and B11, and Request B's gray suffix pages P6 to P8 point to private blocks B12 to B14.

figures.title: Disaggregated Serving Architecture
figures.caption: **Disaggregated Serving Architecture**: A long-prompt, small-decode-batch regime separates compute-bound prefill instances from memory-bandwidth-bound decode instances, mediated by RDMA KV-cache transfer. Because prefill sets time to first token and decode sets time per output token, each pool is sized for its own token rate. Other batch and context sizes can change the binding resources.
figures.alt: Left to right: a prompt enters a prefill pool labeled compute-bound, sets TTFT, and sized for prompt tokens per second. Each of its three workers, Prefill 0 to 2, shows its work as two wide solid blocks, each a whole-prompt pass. An amber arrow carrying four small KV-cache page tiles, labeled KV cache transfer (RDMA), crosses to a decode pool labeled bandwidth-bound, sets TPOT, and sized for output tokens per second. Each of its three workers, Decode 0 to 2, shows its work as a row of eight narrow cells, each a one-token decode step. The decode pool emits a token stream. A key below names the wide block a whole-prompt pass and the narrow cell a one-token decode step.

figures.title: Tensor parallelism for inference
figures.caption: **Tensor parallelism for inference**: Computation is distributed across devices by splitting tensor operations. Attention heads are partitioned across GPUs, requiring an AllReduce operation to synchronize results. Feed-forward networks use a column-row splitting strategy that requires only one AllReduce synchronization per block. This partition can reduce latency when saved compute exceeds communication cost. The illustrated two-collective layer uses a fast local interconnect; its NVLink label is aggregate bidirectional bandwidth, not the per-direction transfer rate.
figures.alt: Two columns labeled GPU 0 and GPU 1, separated by a dashed divider. In the attention stage, each GPU shows eight head tiles: GPU 0 holds the first four as solid tiles and draws the other four dashed, and GPU 1 holds the second four. From the bottom of each GPU's solid head tiles, labeled first or second half of heads, an amber arrow carries a partial output down into an AllReduce over NVLink bar. In the feed-forward stage, each GPU draws the matrix W1 split down the middle into columns, with its own column slice solid and the other dashed, labeled column slice of W1 plus activation. The matrix W2 is split across the middle into rows, with GPU 0 holding the top rows and GPU 1 the bottom rows, labeled row slice of W2 partial sum; on each GPU a blue arrow marked no communication runs from its column slice of W1 to the row slice of W2 it holds, GPU 1's arrow routing around the dashed top rows to enter its bottom rows from the side. Both partial sums feed a second AllReduce bar that leads to the next layer. A key reads held on this GPU for solid tiles and held on the other GPU for dashed tiles.

figures.title: Pipeline parallelism bubbles
figures.caption: **Pipeline parallelism bubbles**: (a) An 80-layer model split into four stages passes one request's activations from stage to stage, so splitting the layers alone does not shorten its sequential computation; it must still traverse all four stages. (b) With many requests in flight, later stages idle during the fill bubble, and from slot t4 onward every stage is busy and one request leaves the pipeline per slot. Pipeline parallelism therefore suits throughput-oriented serving better than latency-critical interactive serving.
figures.alt: Two panels. Top: a request box, four stage boxes labeled GPU 0 to GPU 3 with layer ranges 1 to 20, 21 to 40, 41 to 60, and 61 to 80, and an output box, joined by activation arrows. Hatched fill-bubble cells precede the first request on GPUs 1 to 3, and a dashed line at slot t4 marks the pipeline as full.

figures.title: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing
figures.caption: **Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing**: Expert parallelism distributes \"experts\" across different devices. For each token, a gating mechanism selects the top-$\RoutedExpertCount$ experts. An AllToAll communication step dispatches tokens to the devices hosting their selected experts, the selected experts process the tokens in parallel while experts unselected by this token may serve other tokens, and a second AllToAll step gathers the results for the weighted sum. Distributed expert capacity adds all-to-all communication overhead.
figures.alt: Diagram of MoE token routing for a batch of four tokens, t1 to t4, with t1 drawn solid as the traced token. The batch enters a gate that selects the top two experts per token. Amber lines labeled AllToAll dispatch fan out to three expert cards, one per device: Expert A on device 0 receives t1 and t2, Expert B on device 1 receives t1, t3, and t4, and Expert C on device 2 receives t2, t3, and t4 but not t1. The lines on t1's path, to Experts A and B, are drawn heavier than the thin line to Expert C. Amber lines labeled AllToAll gather return the expert outputs to a weighted-sum box that applies the gate weights and produces the output.

figures.title: Embedding sharding strategies
figures.caption: **Embedding sharding strategies**: Row-wise sharding places complete embedding vectors on specific servers based on entity ID, requiring a network gather for lookup. Column-wise sharding splits each vector across all servers, allowing parallel local lookups followed by an AllGather, which is efficient for popular \"hot\" embeddings. Hybrid sharding combines these approaches, using replication or column sharding for hot items and row sharding for the \"cold\" long tail to balance load and memory.
figures.alt: Three panels, each drawing an embedding table as a grid of rows (one row per ID, numbered 0 to 7 at the left) and columns (dimensions). Panel a, row-wise: server 1 holds whole rows 0 to 3 and server 2 holds whole rows 4 to 7, labeled IDs split, AllToAll, whole vectors. Panel b, column-wise: server 1 and server 2 each hold a tall block of columns spanning all rows 0 to 7, labeled dimensions split, AllGather, slices of each vector. Panel c, hybrid: both servers hold the same shaded hot rows 0 and 1, while server 1 holds cold rows 2 to 4 and server 2 holds cold rows 5 to 7, labeled hot rows replicated, AllToAll, cold tail only.

figures.title: Horizontal scaling with shard groups
figures.caption: **Horizontal scaling with shard groups**: The load balancer treats each shard group as a single logical inference server and chooses among groups by round-robin, two-choice, or session-affinity routing. Within a group, eight GPUs hold the tensor-parallel weight shards and join partial results with an NVLink AllReduce inside every layer, which the router never sees. Adding ready groups raises aggregate capacity; the group's internal parallelism affects per-request latency.
figures.alt: Requests 1, 2, through N feed a violet Load balancer box listing round-robin, two-choice, or session affinity. One arrow per group fans out to Shard group 0, drawn in full detail, and to lighter dashed outlines for Shard groups 1 through N. Shard group 0, labeled one replica, TP = 8, one node, shows eight numbered GPU tiles, each attached by a short link to an amber ring labeled NVLink AllReduce every layer; the other groups repeat the same ring in miniature. Beneath group 0 a note reads TP inside the group sets latency, and an arrow beneath the other groups reads add groups: more aggregate throughput.

figures.title: Circuit breaker states
figures.caption: **Circuit breaker states**: The circuit breaker protects the system from cascading failure. Closed: normal operation. Open: error threshold exceeded; all requests fail fast to prevent resource exhaustion. Half-open: after a timeout, a limited number of requests are allowed through to probe the dependency's health. Success resets to closed; failure returns to open.
figures.alt: State diagram with three rectangular state blocks, each dominated by a switch drawn as a thick hinged blade between two ring terminals, on a wire from the caller to a dependency box. The green closed state, normal traffic, shows the blade closed across both terminals, with two requests arriving and a third crossing the blade toward the dependency. It transitions to the red open state, requests fail fast, when an error, timeout, or latency threshold is exceeded; the open state shows the blade raised, an x mark in the gap, and a single arriving request turned straight back by a red arrow toward the caller, with nothing queued and nothing reaching the dependency. After a timeout, open transitions to the gray half-open state, limited probes, whose blade is closed but whose wire carries a probe limit bar: two requests wait behind the bar while a single probe crosses the switch toward the dependency. Half-open returns to closed when the probe succeeds or to open when the probe fails. A key identifies the dot as a request, the bar as the probe limit, and the small box as the dependency.

figures.title: Bulkhead isolation patterns
figures.caption: **Bulkhead isolation patterns**: To prevent cascading failures in multi-tenant systems, bulkheads isolate resources. Deployment-level bulkheads (shown) assign dedicated physical replicas to high-priority tenants, separating their compute and memory pools. Request-level bulkheads enforce strict concurrency limits within shared processes. Shared networking, storage, and control-plane dependencies remain possible paths for interference.
figures.alt: Two side-by-side compartments, standard tier on the left and gold tier on the right, separated by a thick dark wall labeled bulkhead and both standing on a shared floor band divided into network, storage, and control plane segments. Each tier's traffic enters from above through its own load balancer. Every replica is drawn as a node of four GPU tiles above a memory pool bar. The standard tier has three replicas; the one against the bulkhead is red, crossed out, receives only a dashed line, and is labeled engine crash, and a pale red dashed region marking its blast radius ends flush at the bulkhead wall. The gold tier's two replicas are unaffected and labeled keeps serving. A red dashed line labeled interference path runs from the crashed replica down into the shared floor, passes under the bulkhead, and rises into a gold replica. A key identifies the GPU tile, the memory pool bar, and the blast radius shading.

figures.title: Predictive vs. reactive scaling
figures.caption: **Predictive vs. reactive scaling**: Reactive scaling (gray line) responds to traffic spikes after they occur, leaving a capacity deficit (red region) during cold start in this scenario. Predictive scaling (green line) anticipates traffic and begins provisioning before the spike peaks, shrinking that deficit to a brief, small shortfall at onset in the illustrated forecast. Its early ramp does not eliminate every interval when demand exceeds capacity.
figures.alt: Two time-series panels stacked on a shared time axis and a shared vertical axis of normalized demand or capacity, each showing the same dashed demand curve that rises to a spike and falls back. Panel (a), reactive scaling: a gray capacity line stays flat until near the peak, where a dotted marker labeled scale-up begins sits, then ramps up after demand has already risen; the large region where demand exceeds this capacity is shaded red and labeled capacity deficit. Panel (b), predictive scaling: a green capacity line is marked scale-up begins early in the rise and climbs ahead of demand toward the peak; only a thin red sliver at the onset, labeled brief, small shortfall, shows demand briefly above capacity before the ramp overtakes it.

figures.title: Spot-aware traffic distribution
figures.caption: **Spot-aware traffic distribution**: The gateway classifies requests by SLO and routes 70 percent of traffic, the SLO-critical share, to on-demand replicas that face no spot reclamation, and 30 percent, the best-effort share, to discounted spot replicas that can be preempted. When a spot worker receives an eviction notice, the gateway stops routing to it while it drains, and best-effort requests tolerate occasional retries. The traffic split is illustrative; cost savings depend on provisioned capacity, discounts, retries, and idle headroom.
figures.alt: A Requests box, tagged with an SLO class, feeds a violet Spot-aware gateway box that classifies SLO, watches preemption, and drains. Below it, traffic leaves the gateway as pale gray lanes, each from its own exit point along the gateway's lower edge and ending in an arrowhead at a worker, with combined width proportional to each share. Three wider lanes labeled SLO-critical (70%) fan out to the three reserved workers, 0 to 2, of an On-demand pool with no spot reclamation. Two thinner lanes labeled best-effort (30%) reach spot workers 3 and 4 of a dashed Spot pool, discounted and preemptible; Worker 5, drawn red and dashed and marked draining, receives no lane. A red dashed arrow labeled eviction notice runs from Worker 5 back to the gateway.

figures.title: Serving deployment stack
figures.caption: **Serving deployment stack**: A cache miss crosses three tiers before reaching a model replica. Tier 1 edge points of presence (PoPs) enforce authorization and reuse eligibility before answering repeated requests from cache; a miss passes to Tier 2, where the gateway applies rate limits and authentication and the router picks a destination; Tier 3 GPU workers run prefill and decode while an autoscaler sizes the fleet from queue depth and KV cache use. Tokens stream back up through the tiers to the client. The per-tier latency budgets on the right, drawn on a log scale, are illustrative.

A thick green line labeled token stream rises from decode straight back up through all three tiers to the client. Supporting elements are drawn lighter: two dashed sibling PoPs in Tier 1, a telemetry card in Tier 2, and in Tier 3 two dashed sibling workers fed by a dashed arrow from an autoscaler card driven by queue depth and KV use. On the right, a latency budget column draws one bar per tier on a log scale, labeled under 10 ms, under 50 ms, and under 2 s, so the Tier 3 bar is longest.

figures.title: Global load balancing across inference regions
figures.caption: **Global load balancing across inference regions**: A global load balancer routes each user to an eligible region with suitable latency and ready capacity (@tbl-rtt-by-user-location gives the round-trip times this avoids). Each region (US-East, EU-West, Asia-Pacific) runs independent replicas of the same model, and EU requests can stay in the EU to meet data-residency rules. A shared model registry supplies versioned weights to every region. If a region fails, the load balancer reroutes its users only to destinations that still satisfy placement, readiness, and capacity requirements.

A pale indigo column labeled EU data-residency zone runs behind the EU users, their heavier blue path through the shared load balancer, and the EU-West region, whose role reads EU data stays in region. figures.title: Cache hit and cache miss paths at the edge
figures.caption: **Cache hit and cache miss paths at the edge**: A query first reaches the nearest edge point of presence (PoP). After enforcing authorization and reuse eligibility, the edge targets a cache-hit response in under 10 ms without touching a GPU. On a miss, the request passes through the regional gateway to the central GPU cluster, which runs prefill and decode. Generated tokens stream back to the user, and a response eligible for reuse can be stored at the edge for later queries. The saving depends on the rate of requests eligible for reuse; open-ended generation may offer few such requests.

The arrows are labeled query, miss, and forward. A green path above the row returns from the Edge PoP to the User, labeled cache hit, returned from edge in under 10 ms. A navy path below the row returns from the GPU cluster to the User, labeled cache miss, generated tokens stream back. A dashed green branch from that path goes up into the Edge PoP, labeled store response.

On a miss, the request passes through the regional gateway to the central GPU cluster, which runs prefill and decode. Generated tokens stream back to the user, and a response eligible for reuse can be stored at the edge for later queries. The saving depends on the rate of requests eligible for reuse; open-ended generation may offer few such requests.

figures.title: Ranking cascade architecture
figures.caption: **Ranking cascade architecture**: To optimize latency and cost, search and recommendation systems use a cascade of increasingly complex models. Early stages (Retrieval) filter millions of candidates down to thousands using fast, cheap heuristics. Later stages use expensive, high-precision models only on the most promising candidates.
figures.alt: A funnel of four stacked trapezoid bands that narrow from top to bottom and deepen in blue, with band widths proportional to the logarithm of the candidate count. Retrieval, using lexical and ANN embeddings, cuts 1,000,000 candidates to 10,000; first-stage ranking, using two-tower models and GBDTs, cuts 10,000 to 1,000; second-stage scoring, using deep MLPs and DLRM, cuts 1,000 to 100; and final re-ranking, using a cross-attention transformer, cuts 100 to 10. A separate column of horizontal bars, with length proportional to the latency budget, grows downward as the funnel shrinks: at most 10 ms, about 20 ms, about 50 ms, and about 100 ms.

figures.title: Local-only, centralized-cloud, and federated learning
figures.caption: **Local-only, centralized-cloud, and federated learning**: The panels compare three architectures by what crosses the device boundary (dashed line), rather than imply a required evolution. (A) Local-only learning trains on the device and sends nothing. (B) Centralized-cloud learning uploads raw data to a cloud trainer. (C) Federated learning keeps data on the device, downloads the global model $\ModelParameters$, and uploads only model updates $\FiniteChange\ModelParameters$ to a federated averaging (FedAvg) coordinator. Data locality in (C) still requires separate privacy controls for updates and metadata.
figures.alt: Three panels separated by a dashed device boundary line. Each device box holds a small grid of green data records. Panel A, local only: one device with a self-loop arrow labeled train and an empty dashed box labeled no server. Panel B, centralized cloud: three devices send amber arrows carrying green record tiles up to a cloud trainer that holds a pooled grid of all the records. Panel C, federated: three devices keep their records, send amber delta theta arrows up to a FedAvg coordinator holding global theta, and receive gray theta arrows down. Footers read nothing leaves the device, raw data leaves the device, and only model updates leave.

figures.title: Adaptation memory budget

figures.title: The edge inference landscape
figures.caption: **The edge inference landscape**: Published inference latency and energy measurements from MLPerf Tiny and official benchmarks reveal three distinct hardware tiers separated by approximately 100$\times$ in energy per inference; because the tiers run different workloads (keyword spotting and small-image tasks versus ResNet-50), the gap mixes hardware efficiency with workload size. Dedicated neural processors (Syntiant, STM32N6) achieve keyword spotting in under 5 ms at 30--160 microjoules, while edge GPUs (Jetson Orin) deliver sub-millisecond latency at 15 mJ.
figures.alt: Log-log scatter plot of inference latency in milliseconds against energy per inference in microjoules. A light gray band labeled MCU/ASIC tier holds Syntiant Core 2 and STM32N6 NPU points from tens to a few hundred microjoules; a slightly darker gray band labeled edge accelerator tier holds Google Coral Edge TPU at a few thousand microjoules; the darkest gray band, labeled edge GPU tier, holds Jetson AGX Orin running ResNet-50 near 15000 microjoules at under one millisecond. A double-headed arrow at the left spanning the bands is labeled about 100 times energy gap.

figures.title: TinyTL adaptation paths
figures.caption: **TinyTL adaptation paths**: (A) Full fine-tuning updates every weight and retains the state needed for their gradients. figures.title: LoRA architecture
figures.caption: **LoRA architecture**: The input $\LayerInputVector$ passes through the frozen base matrix $\WeightMatrix_0$ and, in parallel, through a trainable low-rank path: down-projection $\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ ($\AdapterRank \times \HiddenDimension$) and up-projection $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix$ ($\HiddenDimension \times \AdapterRank$), which play the roles of $\LowRankRightFactor^T$ and $\LowRankLeftFactor$ in the low-rank update above. Only $\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ and $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix$ carry gradients and optimizer state. For serving, the product $\AdapterUpProjectionMatrix\AdapterDownProjectionMatrix$ can be folded into $\WeightMatrix_0$, removing the separate adapter operations when the merged representation is supported. End-to-end latency still needs measurement.
figures.alt: Matrices drawn to proportion. Input vector x of length d splits into two paths. The upper path passes through a large gray frozen square W0 of size d by d to the vector W0 x. The lower path passes through a short wide blue matrix A of size r by d, a tiny vector of length r, and a tall thin blue matrix B of size d by r to the vector BA x. The two vectors add at a plus node to give output h of length d. To the right, a separate panel labeled for serving shows one d by d matrix W0 plus BA with the adapter folded in. A legend marks gray as frozen, with no gradients or optimizer state, and blue as trainable.

figures.title: Federated averaging protocol
figures.caption: **Federated averaging protocol**: One FedAvg round in four steps. (1) The coordinator selects a cohort, over-selecting to absorb dropouts, and broadcasts the global model $\ModelParameters^{\FederatedRoundIndex}$. (2) Each client runs $\LocalEpochCount$ local epochs on its private data. (3) Clients that finish before the round deadline upload $\ModelParameters_k^{\FederatedRoundIndex+1}$; a straggler that misses the deadline is dropped. (4) The coordinator forms the example-weighted average of @eq-fedavg-weighted-aggregation, which becomes the next global model.
figures.alt: A round drawn on a time axis. A coordinator lane at the top holds step 1, select cohort and broadcast theta t, and step 4, aggregate as a sum of n k over n round times theta k at t plus 1. A gray broadcast line feeds five client lanes. Each client lane shows a green local data block whose width reflects its example count, then a blue bar of E local epochs and an amber upload block. Circled step numbers 2 and 3 sit above the first client's epoch bar and upload block. Clients 1 to 4 finish before a red dashed round deadline, and their uploads join an amber line into the aggregate step. Client 5's bar runs past the deadline into a red hatched segment marked with a cross and labeled dropped.

figures.title: Measuring the local-work trade-off
figures.caption: **Measuring the local-work trade-off**: The local-work setting $\LocalEpochCount$ acts through two opposing paths. More local epochs lengthen each round, $\RoundDuration(\LocalEpochCount)$, while reducing how often clients synchronize, which can lower the rounds to target, $\FederatedRoundCount(\LocalEpochCount)$, unless client drift raises it. Only their combination, the measured time to target $\TimeToTarget(\LocalEpochCount)$, ranks candidate settings, and a setting is admissible only if it also fits the client energy and population-coverage budgets.
figures.alt: Three rows on a common wall-clock time axis, for small, moderate, and large E. Each row is a sequence of rounds, each a blue local-epochs segment followed by an amber upload and sync segment. The small-E row has many short rounds with thin blue segments; the moderate-E row has fewer, longer rounds; the large-E row has three long rounds plus one more round added by drift, its local-epochs segment gray hatched and still ending in an amber sync segment. A bracket over the first row is labeled rounds to target R of E, and a bracket under one large-E round is labeled round duration t r of E. Each row ends at a tick labeled T target of E; the moderate row ends first and its tick is green.

figures.title: Communication-computation trade-off in federated learning
figures.caption: **Communication-computation trade-off in federated learning**: As network bandwidth decreases from fast to slow, the time-minimizing number of local epochs shifts rightward because additional local computation amortizes more communication. The curves come from an illustrative cost model in relative units, not measurements; its growing local-work term stands in for the longer rounds and added drift that make excessive local work counterproductive.

An arrow in a band beneath the plotting area, under the feet of the droplines, runs from E star equals 10 to E star equals 40 and is labeled slower network, larger E star.

figures.title: Gradient compression techniques
figures.caption: **Gradient compression techniques**: Standard updates transmit full-precision values; quantization maps values to lower-precision buckets, such as FP32 to INT8; and sparsification transmits only the most significant top-$\Glyph{k}$ gradients. The latter two mechanisms reduce bytes transferred but introduce representation error or residual state that the training algorithm must manage.
figures.alt: Three rows, each showing a four-value gradient vector on the left and its upload payload as a horizontal bar on the right. Row A, FP32: values plus 0.50, minus 0.20, plus 0.01, plus 0.80, each 32 bits, giving a 128-bit bar. Row B, INT8 with scale s about 0.0063: values plus 79, minus 32, plus 2, plus 127, each 8 bits, giving a bar one quarter as long plus a small hatched scale segment. Row C, top-k with k equal to 2: values at index 0 and 3 are kept, the two dropped values are dashed and flow down into a residual e box kept on the device, and the bar holds two values plus a hatched index segment.

figures.title: Federated personalization architectures
figures.caption: **Federated personalization architectures**: (A) Full fine-tuning updates every layer; (B) head-only adaptation freezes the feature extractor and trains only the task head; (C) adapter-based learning, such as LoRA, inserts small trainable modules beside a frozen backbone. The dashed arrow marks how far the backward pass must reach. Adapters shrink trainable state, but because they sit at every depth their gradients still traverse the backbone, so the required backward state must be retained or recomputed. In this comparison, head-only adaptation truncates the backward pass at the feature extractor.

To the left of each column, hatched tiles mark where backward state is kept or recomputed: beside every layer and the head in columns A and C, beside the head only in column B. A legend marks gray as frozen, blue as trainable, the dashed arrow as backward pass extent, and the hatched tile as state kept or recomputed.

figures.title: Secure aggregation protocol
figures.caption: **Secure aggregation protocol**: A simplified two-client view of pairwise masking. Clients A and B agree on a shared random mask $\PairwiseMaskSecret$; A uploads $\FirstClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters + \PairwiseMaskSecret$ and B uploads $\SecondClientMaskedUpdate = \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters - \PairwiseMaskSecret$, so each upload alone looks random to the server. Summing them cancels the mask and yields exactly $\FiniteChange\FirstClientModelParameters + \FiniteChange\SecondClientModelParameters$. The server learns only the aggregate, which can still leak information unless differential privacy bounds it.
figures.alt: Each update is drawn as a row of six shaded cells. Client A's update delta theta A, a smooth pattern of blue cells, passes through a plus s node to produce y A, an irregular pattern of amber cells labeled looks random; client B's update delta theta B passes through a minus s node to produce y B, also labeled looks random, whose cells are lightest where the mask is darkest and y A's cells are darkest. Between the clients, a row of irregular gray cells is the shared mask s from key agreement, linked by dashed lines to both mask nodes. Amber uplinks cross a dashed boundary from on device to visible to server. Inside the aggregation server, y A and y B are added like a column sum, giving a row of green cells equal to delta theta A plus delta theta B, with the note masks cancel, s minus s equals 0.

figures.title: Tiered adaptation strategy
figures.caption: **Tiered adaptation strategy**: The flowchart routes a deployment by the adaptation the local change needs, then by whether a larger update is needed for the quality target and fits the measured device budget, then by whether updates are valuable across devices. Bias-only updates, adapters or LoRA, and partial or full fine-tuning are candidates for increasingly demanding changes on increasingly capable devices, subject to measured resource and quality budgets. The federated card names one common configuration; whether differential privacy is required depends on the deployment's threat model.
figures.alt: Flowchart starting at deploy on-device learning. Diamond one asks whether heavy adaptation is needed: no leads down to the first of three adaptation cards lined up left to right; yes leads to diamond two, compute and energy sufficient, whose no branch leads to the second card and whose yes branch leads to the third. Each card carries a small branch tag at its top, lightweight, moderate, and full from left to right, and is drawn around a large four-layer stack whose blue trainable share grows from left to right: bias-only BitFit on microcontrollers shows gray layers each holding a small blue chip labeled b; adapters or LoRA on mobile NPUs shows gray layers each with a blue adapter beside it; partial or full fine-tuning on wall-powered edge servers and high-end GPUs shows all four layers blue. All three cards join into diamond three, updates valuable across devices: no leads to a local-only adaptation card, shadow validation and drift monitoring, marked by one device with a self-loop arrow; yes leads to a violet federated card, FedAvg plus differential privacy, fleet model synchronization, marked by three devices sending amber arrows up to a global theta box.

figures.actual_question: How should adaptation demand and device limits guide deployment?
figures.actual_scope: The cards describe candidate adaptation methods, not rigid device tiers. Every branch still requires measured quality, memory, runtime, and energy feasibility.

actual_steps.title: Ask what change is needed
actual_steps.description: A light adaptation need routes toward bias-only updates. A powerful device does not make a larger update necessary if the smaller method meets the quality target.

actual_steps.title: Admit a larger candidate
actual_steps.description: A heavier change requires checking whether the larger update fits compute and energy limits. The moderate adapter branch remains a candidate when full fine-tuning is unnecessary or infeasible.

actual_steps.title: Check whether sharing helps
actual_steps.description: Only after selecting an adaptation candidate does the flow ask whether updates are valuable across devices. This determines whether federation is useful.

actual_steps.title: Choose an operational policy
actual_steps.description: Local-only deployment uses local validation and monitoring; federation adds coordination and appropriate privacy controls. The named differential-privacy configuration is not mandatory for every threat model.

actual_steps.description: The device keeps local data and adapts the permitted model components. Versioned weights alone no longer describe every behavior that can emerge.

actual_steps.title: Return governed evidence
actual_steps.description: Telemetry supplies aggregate metrics through privacy controls. Keeping raw data local does not make those returned metrics inherently private.

actual_steps.description: The dashed feedback path can trigger cloud retraining when the evidence warrants it. A detected change must first be distinguished from an actual quality regression.

figures.title: On-device shadow validation
figures.caption: **On-device shadow validation**: A frozen baseline runs beside the active model. Their disagreement, confidence, latency, and resource deltas can flag a change without labels; a rollback decision still requires a validated outcome signal or safety invariant.
figures.alt: Eight live inputs, x1 to x8, form columns. In each column the gray frozen baseline, v1 in shadow, and the blue adapted candidate, v1.1 serving, each emit a class letter. A box labeled validated outcome or safety invariant feeds the gate, which resolves either to a green clear, return to service, or a red regression, roll back.

figures.title: The N-models complexity explosion
figures.caption: **The N-models complexity explosion**: The curves show monitoring alerts growing linearly with model count, deployment coordination growing as $\mathcal{O}(\ProductionModelCount \log \ProductionModelCount)$, and dependency conflicts growing quadratically as models share features and data sources. Under these assumed shapes, the total operational load crosses team capacity around 50 models, sketching the transition from artisanal model management to platform-required operations.
figures.alt: Log-log plot of operational load against models in production. A dotted linear monitoring line, a dashed model-count-log-model-count deployment line, and a dash-dot quadratic dependency line sum to a solid total curve that crosses a red dashed team-capacity line at about 50 models, marked with a red dot. figures.title: Feature store architecture
figures.caption: **Feature store architecture**: A dual-store architecture resolves the conflict between training (high-throughput batch scans) and serving (low-latency point lookups). One set of feature definitions drives materialization from batch and streaming sources into an offline store, which keeps full history for point-in-time training joins (the throughput path, top), and an online store, which keeps the latest value per entity for serving lookups (the latency path, bottom). Shared definitions support compatible feature meanings; materialization and historical-availability checks must verify that contract.
figures.alt: A violet feature definitions box sends a dashed arrow into a tall green materialization box listing batch, streaming, and on-demand, which batch data and event streams feed from the left. The offline store is drawn as a grid of cells, rows by entity and columns by time, labeled full history with a time arrow; a bracket over all its rows sends an arrow labeled scan to a blue training box labeled point-in-time joins, under the heading throughput path. The online store is drawn as three key cells, each with one latest-value cell; one value cell is outlined and sends an arrow labeled lookup to a blue serving box labeled point lookups, under the heading latency path.

figures.title: Point-in-time correctness
figures.caption: **Point-in-time correctness**: A training example at noon should see only the clicks already logged by noon (solid green, 4), not the clicks that arrive later (dashed gray). A naive join that reads the midnight batch value of `total_clicks_today` counts all 10 and leaks six future events into the example. A point-in-time join pairs each training event with feature values as they existed *at the event timestamp*, so the example contains only information that would have been available at inference time.

A green bracket spans the four early clicks, labeled 4 clicks, with an arrow to a green box reading point-in-time join, total_clicks_today equals 4. A red dashed bracket spans all ten clicks, labeled 10 clicks by midnight, with an arrow to a red box reading naive join, midnight value, total_clicks_today equals 10.

figures.title: Shadow and canary deployment
figures.caption: **Shadow and canary deployment**: In shadow deployment (A), the proxy mirrors all production traffic to the candidate; users receive only the production response, and both outputs are compared offline. No user sees the candidate's output, but mirroring every request doubles inference load, so the shadow path needs its own capacity and must be isolated so it cannot slow production. In canary deployment (B), the splitter sends a small weighted slice of live traffic to the candidate (here the 5 percent stage) and widens it through the 1, 5, 25, 50, and 100 percent stages as evidence accumulates, rolling back if SLO or error metrics drift.
figures.alt: Two panels. Panel A, shadow deployment: live traffic enters an amber traffic proxy. One lane carries a row of 20 solid request ticks labeled every request to the production model, whose output becomes the user response; a second dashed lane carries 20 hollow ticks labeled every request, copied, to a dashed candidate shadow model, labeled 2 times inference load, whose output is logged but not returned. Both outputs feed a violet offline diff box comparing outputs and latency. Panel B, canary deployment: live traffic enters an amber traffic splitter. The production lane, labeled 95 percent, carries 19 of the 20 request ticks with one empty slot, and the candidate canary lane, labeled 5 percent, carries the single tick from that slot. Beside it, five bars drawn to scale show canary shares of 1, 5, 25, 50, and 100 percent with the 5 percent bar highlighted, above a red dashed box reading roll back if SLO or error metrics drift.

figures.title: Interleaving vs. A/B testing
figures.caption: **Interleaving vs. A/B testing**: (A) A/B testing splits users into cohorts, and each cohort sees only one ranker's list, so the comparison is between cohort means and must overcome the variation between users. (B) Interleaving has both rankers rank the same query for each user and merges the results into one list (here by team draft); each click is credited to the ranker that contributed the item, so every user supplies a paired, within-user comparison. That pairing can make ranker-preference screening more sample-efficient; it does not measure the full deployment outcome assessed by an A/B test [@netflix2017interleaving].
figures.alt: Two panels. Panel A, A/B testing: a row of eight user circles, four blue labeled cohort 1 at 50 percent and four gray labeled cohort 2 at 50 percent. Cohort 1 sees a list of blue items A1 to A3 labeled ranker A only, cohort 2 sees gray items B1 to B3 labeled ranker B only, and each list leads to its own mean box; a bracket joins the two means above the label compare the two cohorts' means. Panel B, interleaving: a box reading each user, one query feeds ranker A's blue list A1 to A3 and ranker B's gray list B1 to B3, which merge into one middle list labeled merged list alternating A1, B1, A2, B2, with a thin connector from each source item to its merged slot. A click dot on the edge of merged A2 routes to a credit A box and a click dot on the edge of merged B2 routes to a credit B box; a bracket joins them above the label credit each click to its source ranker.

An owner column lists incident lead, domain teams, model owners, and platform team. A key reads page and diagnostic record.

figures.title: Organizational patterns for ML
figures.caption: **Organizational patterns for ML**: (A) A centralized platform team gives every model team the same infrastructure, but all requests pass through one shared queue, which can become the bottleneck. (B) Embedded teams each build their own tooling, which is fast locally but duplicates infrastructure and lets stacks diverge. (C) A hybrid keeps a core platform and places ML engineers (MLE) inside model teams as liaisons, balancing standardization with responsiveness.

Panel C, hybrid: one violet core platform box sends an arrow down into each team box, where it ends at a violet MLE chip inside the team.

figures.title: Threat prioritization matrix
figures.caption: **Threat prioritization matrix**: Likelihood and impact place each example threat in a quadrant, and the quadrant sets the response. Likely, damaging threats such as federated data poisoning warrant automated defenses; rare but severe threats such as hardware side channels justify preparation in high-value deployments; likely but lower-impact extraction calls for API limits; and membership inference through a public API is monitored and reassessed when the training data is sensitive. Dashed arrows show how deployment assumptions move a threat to another quadrant.
figures.alt: Likelihood and impact plane split into four quadrants, with the high-likelihood, high-impact quadrant shaded red. Each quadrant names a response and holds one example threat as a dot: automate defenses for data poisoning in federated training, prepare where value is high for hardware side channels on cloud-hosted models, limit and shape the API for model extraction via a public API, and monitor and reassess for membership inference via a public API. Two dashed arrows move threats to new positions: side channels shift right toward higher likelihood with sensitive co-tenants or exposed edge hardware, and membership inference shifts up toward higher impact with sensitive training data.

figures.title: Model theft strategies
figures.caption: **Model theft strategies**: Exact artifact theft (left) obtains the model file, checkpoint, registry entry, or device artifact and reconstructs the original model. Approximate behavioral theft (right) uses black-box API queries, output signals, and surrogate training or distillation to clone the model's behavior without direct access to weights.
figures.alt: Two panels. Left, exact artifact theft: a registry, bucket, or device frame holds a shaded weight grid; a red arrow labeled access the file, extract weights leads to a red exact-copy box with an identical grid, captioned same weights, no training cost paid. Right, approximate behavioral theft: a table of recorded x and y pairs sends queries to a dark deployed-API box and receives labels, logits, and scores; a red arrow labeled train surrogate leads to a red behavioral-clone box with a differently shaded grid, captioned different weights, similar outputs.

figures.title: Data poisoning as bilevel optimization
figures.caption: **Data poisoning as bilevel optimization**: The attacker (outer loop) chooses poisoning data $\PoisoningDataset$ to raise the trained model's loss on a test set, the untargeted form drawn here, or, for a targeted attack, to lower its loss on the attacker's chosen label. The system (inner loop) attempts to minimize its training loss on the combined dataset $\CleanTrainingDataset \cup \PoisoningDataset$. The nested attack objective can require repeated training evaluations or approximations. It does not imply that every poisoning defense must simulate full training.
figures.alt: A red attacker box at top holds the outer objective, maximizing test loss over the poison set subject to a size budget. A red arrow labeled inject leads to a grid of training tiles in which three red poisoned tiles sit among clean tiles, labeled S union S poison. A blue arrow leads to the inner-loop training box with the arg-min training equation and a chain of SGD steps ending at theta star. A theta-star arrow feeds an evaluation box that computes the target test loss, and a red feedback arrow returns the target loss along the right edge to the attacker.

figures.title: Data Poisoning Impact
figures.caption: **Data Poisoning Impact**: A nominal pipeline (top) and a poisoned pipeline (bottom) pass through the same four stages. In the illustrated successful attack, a poisoned record admitted at ingestion contaminates the training corpus, pulls the optimizer's gradients toward the attacker's trigger, and yields a backdoored model whose clean accuracy can remain intact, so aggregate validation alone can miss it.
figures.alt: Two rows of four panels under the headings ingestion, training corpus, optimization, and trained model, joined by arrows. In the nominal row, three green clean records arrive, the corpus is a grid of green record tiles, a gray step descends into the minimum of a set of loss contours, and a straight decision boundary separates hollow and filled points. In the poisoned row, the middle arriving record is red, one tile of the corpus grid is red, a red step bends away from the contour minimum toward a red trigger diamond while a dashed gray path shows the clean direction, and the same decision boundary now has a small red dashed pocket around a trigger diamond on the filled side, labeled backdoor pocket and clean accuracy intact. The arrows in the poisoned row are red.

figures.title: Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation
figures.caption: **Collaborative Poisoning via Aggregation**: In a collaborative learning setting, multiple clients each train on local data and contribute model updates to a central server that aggregates them into a shared global model. A single malicious participant can inject poisoned updates that the server folds into the aggregated model, so the corruption spreads to every client without any one obvious anomaly. This attack surface differs from adversarial examples because it targets the model during *training* rather than at *inference*.
figures.alt: A violet aggregation server box at the top shows the weighted mean w t plus 1 equals w t plus the sum over k of n k over n times delta w k, and an inset plot of update vectors drawn from the point w t: three amber honest updates point steeply upward in a narrow fan, one red update delta w 2 points nearly sideways, and a thicker violet aggregate arrow sits between them, tilted away from the honest fan. A row of clients sits below: client 1, a red malicious client 2, client 3, an ellipsis, and client N, each holding a row of small green data tiles, with two red tiles in client 2. Each benign client sends an amber update arrow, delta w 1, delta w 3, and delta w N, up to the server, while client 2 sends a red update delta w 2 marked poisoned. Dashed red arrows labeled w t plus 1 run from the server down to each client.

figures.title: Adversarial arms race
figures.caption: **Adversarial arms race**: Defense evaluation is an iterative engineering cycle of defining the adversary's capabilities, evaluating adaptive attacks against active defenses, revising mechanisms and assumptions, and retesting after system or deployment modifications. The diagram formalizes the review process rather than predicting defense longevity.
figures.alt: Four numbered cards at the corners around a central system, a model box inside a green defense boundary with a gap on its right side. Card 1, specify the adversary, shows white, gray, and black box access and a perturbation budget and goal; a gray arrow leads to card 2, run adaptive attacks, drawn in red, whose red arrow passes through the gap in the defense and strikes the model. A gray arrow labeled results leads to card 3, harden the system, whose green arrow returns to the defense boundary. A gray arrow from the changed system leads to card 4, retest after changes to weights, data, or deployment, where the line earlier evidence is struck through, and a gray arrow returns to card 1.

figures.title: Adversarial decision boundary
figures.caption: **Adversarial decision boundary**: High-dimensional neural networks often have nonlinear decision boundaries. An adversary seeks to find a minimal perturbation $\Glyph{\boldsymbol{\delta}}$ that pushes a clean data point $\ModelInput$ across the boundary into another class region, subject to an allowed perturbation bound $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$. A norm bound alone does not establish perceptual invisibility; physical attacks require separate feasibility constraints.

figures.title: Threat mitigation flow
figures.caption: **Threat mitigation flow**: Threats, assessment evidence, and candidate controls have different roles. figures.alt: Four threat rows, each with red-dot threat, blue assessment-evidence chips, and green candidate-control chips, with a solid line from each threat to its evidence chips and dashed lines from every evidence chip to every control chip in the row. Model extraction: query telemetry to access and query limits and output restrictions. Data poisoning: provenance audit and targeted evaluations, crossing to intake controls and quarantine and retraining. Adversarial input: adaptive attack tests to adversarial training and input validation. Membership inference: privacy attack audit and privacy accounting to an accounted DP mechanism.

figures.title: Hardware supply chain attack surface
figures.caption: **Hardware supply chain attack surface**: Each lifecycle stage admits its own compromise (red arrows) and needs its own assurance evidence (green gates); no single check covers the chain, and dashed lines carry each missed compromise forward to deployment. Unlike software, which can be patched remotely, a compromise that survives to deployment often requires physical replacement.
figures.alt: A left-to-right pipeline of five stage boxes: design, fabrication, assembly, distribution, deployment. Above each stage a red arrow labeled with its compromise strikes a green gate box naming its assurance check: design flaws or malicious IP hit design review and verification, hardware Trojans hit die inspection by micrography, substituted components hit X-ray screening, cloned or relabeled parts hit provenance and functional tests, and probing and fault injection hit secure boot and attestation. Below the pipeline, dashed red lines marked if missed leave the first four stage boxes and run to deployment, where they end at a red bracket labeled physical replacement.

figures.title: Layered defense stack
figures.caption: **Layered defense stack**: Controls are grouped by the layer they protect, from the silicon root of trust through platform isolation and model safeguards to data privacy. A compromised component can undermine controls that rely on its execution or stored state. These runtime dependencies must be checked against each control’s threat model; a correctly released differentially private artifact retains its release-level guarantee.
figures.alt: Four stacked tiers of four controls each. From top: data (encryption at rest, provenance tracking, secure aggregation, differential privacy), model (adversarial training, input validation, output monitoring, rate limits), platform (container isolation, network segmentation, access control, runtime telemetry), and hardware (trusted execution, secure boot, HSM key custody, PUF device identity). A red dot on the platform tier marked compromised host sends a dashed red arrow up to the differential privacy block, labeled alters it before release, while a green arrow from differential privacy leads to a separate green released-artifact box.

figures.title: Secure enclave architecture
figures.caption: **Secure enclave architecture**: The Secure Enclave is an isolated region of the system on chip with its own processor, random-number generator, public-key accelerator, AES engine, and root keys. The application processor reaches it only through a mailbox, enclave memory in DRAM passes through a memory protection engine, and storage keys go directly to the inline AES engine, so a compromised application processor never holds them. Source: Apple.
figures.alt: Block diagram. A system-on-chip frame holds an application processor and a Secure Enclave region containing an enclave processor, TRNG, memory protection engine, PKA, AES engine, and root keys. Arrows connect the application processor to DRAM and to the enclave through a mailbox, the memory protection engine to an encrypted enclave region of DRAM, the enclave to secure storage over I2C, and the root keys to a storage AES engine that writes encrypted data to NAND flash.
