figures.title: Secure boot sequence
figures.caption: **Secure boot sequence**: Each trusted stage authenticates the next component before use. Extending the chain to a verified model loader permits model-artifact authentication; generic boot verification does not provide that extension automatically. Measured boot records evidence, whereas verification enforces the loading decision.
figures.alt: Horizontal chain of four stages: 1, immutable boot root; 2, verified bootloader; 3, verified OS or loader; 4, authorized ML workload. Green diamonds between stages authenticate the bootloader, the kernel and startup policy, and the manifest and artifact digest; each diamond sends a red fail arrow up to a shared box labeled halt and reject the component. Below, a measurement log row records bootloader hash, kernel hash, and model digest under stages 2 to 4, and a bracket under the last gate and stage reads extension to the model. A dashed after-boot arrow leads to a dashed box reading runtime controls still required.

figures.title: Weight Corruption via Bit Flip
figures.caption: **Weight Corruption via Bit Flip**: (a) One corrupted weight $\CorruptedModelWeight$ drives hidden unit $\HiddenUnitOutput_2$, whose output feeds every downstream logit. (b) For an illustrative trained weight $\ModelWeight = 0.042 \approx 1.34 \times 2^{-5}$, flipping bit 30, the most significant exponent bit of the FP32 word, raises the stored exponent from $2^{-5}$ to $2^{123}$. In general, flipping an exponent bit with place value $2^{\ExponentBitIndex}$ scales the value by $2^{\pm 2^{\ExponentBitIndex}}$; here the factor is $2^{128}$, giving $\CorruptedModelWeight \approx 1.4 \times 10^{37}$. The result is still finite, so NaN and infinity checks never fire, yet it can produce extreme downstream activations, depending on the input, activation function, and downstream weights. A range check $|\ModelWeight| \le \WeightRangeBound$ against the trained weight distribution catches it cheaply.
figures.alt: Left: a small network with four inputs, three hidden units, and two outputs; one input-to-hidden weight is drawn thick and red, and dashed red arrows run from the affected hidden unit to both outputs. Right: two FP32 bit rows showing sign, eight exponent bits, and a collapsed mantissa. The top row encodes w = 0.042 with exponent bits 01111010; an arrow labeled bit 30 flips 0 to 1, value times 2 to the 128 leads to the bottom row, whose first exponent bit is red and set to 1, labeled w prime approximately 1.4 times 10 to the 37.

figures.caption: **Silent Error Probability at Scale**: Probability of at least one silent data corruption event per hour as a function of cluster size, for three illustrative per-device error rates. figures.alt: Semilog plot showing three S-curves, solid, dashed, and dotted, labeled with per-device SDC rates of 1e-3, 1e-4, and 1e-5. The 1e-3 and 1e-4 curves enter the red band and approach probability 1.0 by 100000 devices, with a dot marking 0.63 at 10K on the 1e-4 curve; the 1e-5 curve rises to about 0.63.

figures.title: The Robustness Taxonomy
figures.caption: **The Robustness Taxonomy**: Environmental shifts, input-level attacks, and system-level faults decomposed into concrete failure subtypes (dark), each paired with its principal defense (green). Each pillar descends onto a defense wall at the point where it enters the ML pipeline, the data stream, the model's inputs and training data, or the weights and accelerators. Software and pipeline defects originate in the system layer, but they are drawn as the cross-cutting pipeline rail on which all three walls sit because their symptoms can amplify or imitate any of the pillars.
figures.alt: Three side-by-side pillar columns sit above one horizontal dashed pipeline band that runs left to right from data in to output and is labeled software and pipeline defects, cross-cutting; inside the band, a labeled icon sits centered under each column. Each column holds four white failure chips, each naming a failure in dark text and its defense in green. A red arrow from each column's chips ends on a solid green wall bar resting on the pipeline band, directly above the component that pillar strikes: a data stream of sample dots under environmental shifts, a grid of input and training data tiles under input-level attacks, and an accelerator chip holding weight cells under system-level faults. Environmental shifts: covariate shift to importance weighting, concept drift to retraining on fresh labels, label shift to prior re-estimation and recalibration, domain shift to domain adaptation and fine-tuning. Input-level attacks: evasion (FGSM, PGD) to adversarial training, C and W and boundary attacks to certified defenses, data and backdoor poisoning to provenance and spectral filtering, physical perturbations to transformation-robust training. System-level faults: silent data corruption to redundant execution and fleet screening, memory and weight bit flips to ECC and weight range checks, underflow overflow and NaN to loss scaling and NaN guards, distributed training desync to checkpoint rollback and watchdogs.

figures.title: Types of Distribution Shift
figures.caption: **Types of Distribution Shift**: (a) Under covariate shift, deployment inputs move to a new region of feature space while the labeling rule, and so the correct boundary, stays fixed. (b) Under label shift, class frequencies change while each class's inputs look the same; the bar heights are illustrative. (c) Under concept drift, the same inputs acquire new labels, so points between the old and new boundaries become errors. Covariate shift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput)$ with $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel \mid \ModelInput)$ fixed, label shift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel)$ with $\ProbabilityFunction(\ModelInput \mid \ExampleLabel)$ fixed, and concept drift changes $\ProbabilityFunction(\ExampleLabel \mid \ModelInput)$; the distinction determines whether reweighting, recalibration, or model adaptation is appropriate.
figures.alt: Three panels with a shared key for class 0 (filled) and class 1 (open) points and red label-changed points. Panel a, covariate shift: blue training points labeled train, of two classes, sit on either side of a dashed boundary, and an arrow points to amber deployment points labeled deploy, of the same two classes in a new region, still on the correct sides of the unchanged boundary. Panel b, label shift: paired blue train and amber deploy bars for y equals 0 and y equals 1; training bars are equal, and the deployment bar for y equals 1 is much taller than for y equals 0. Panel c, concept drift: the same points with a dashed boundary labeled old and a solid green boundary labeled new crossing it; points between the two boundaries are red to mark changed labels.

figures.title: Gradient-Based Attack Geometry
figures.caption: **Gradient-Based Attack Geometry**: Around a correctly classified input $\ModelInput$, the dashed square marks every perturbation allowed by the $\ell_\infty$ budget $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$. FGSM moves each coordinate by the full budget in the sign direction of the loss gradient $\nabla_\ModelInput \LossFunction(\ModelParameters, \ModelInput, \ExampleLabel)$, which lands $\AdversarialExample$ on a corner of that square, the allowed point that maximizes the first-order increase in loss. A step no larger than $\AdversarialPerturbationBudget$ in any coordinate therefore carries the input across the decision boundary. The class labels are illustrative.
figures.alt: Two-dimensional input space divided by a solid diagonal decision boundary into a true-class region and an other-class region. A clean input x sits inside a dashed square labeled allowed set. A short blue arrow labeled gradient of L points up and to the left from x; a longer red arrow runs from x to the square's upper-left corner, marked x adv equals x plus epsilon times sign of the gradient, which lies across the boundary. A bracket under the square marks its half-width epsilon adv.

figures.title: Autoencoder Ingestion Gate
figures.caption: **Autoencoder Ingestion Gate**: An autoencoder trained on trusted data learns to compress inputs through a narrow latent layer $\EncoderLatentRepresentation$ and reconstruct them. Reconstruction error supplies an anomaly score, not proof that an input is poisoned. The gate accepts records whose reconstruction error $\AutoencoderReconstructionError$ stays at or below a threshold $\ResponseThreshold$ calibrated on held-out clean data and quarantines the rest.
figures.alt: Symmetric hourglass network: an encoder narrows seven input units through five and three hidden units to a two-unit latent layer, and a decoder expands back to seven reconstructed outputs. An arrow from the output leads to a reconstruction error panel, L rec equals the squared norm of x minus x hat, containing a horizontal score axis labeled L rec at its arrow end and split by a dashed threshold tau. Left of tau is a green accept zone, L rec at most tau, holding a stacked cluster of green record dots at low scores; right of tau is a red quarantine zone, L rec greater than tau, holding two red record dots at high scores.

figures.title: Model Scaling Laws
figures.caption: **Model Scaling Laws**: In the ranges studied by @kaplan2020scaling, increasing model size, dataset size, and compute consistently reduced test loss. Each law is normalized to its loss at the smallest studied value, so on these log-log axes its slope is its exponent; the dashed staircase on the compute law marks the compute multiple that buys each successive fixed fractional reduction in loss. The figure reproduces source-paper notation, where $\Glyph{N}$ denotes parameter count and $\Glyph{C_{\text{min}}}$ denotes compute; elsewhere this book uses $\Parameters$ for parameter count and $\Operations$ for operation count. These scaling laws explain why larger models, more data, and increased compute became attractive design choices within that regime.
figures.alt: Log-log plot of test loss relative to its starting value against the resource as a multiple of its smallest studied value. Three straight lines start at 1: dataset size in green with exponent minus 0.095 over a hundredfold range, parameters in blue with exponent minus 0.076 over a millionfold range, and compute in orange with exponent minus 0.050 over ten orders of magnitude, ending lowest. A dashed orange staircase of three tinted steps on the compute line is labeled each 10 percent lower loss costs 8.2 times compute.

figures.title: The Energy Gap
figures.caption: **The Energy Gap**: US data center electricity consumption more than tripled from `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2014_twh_str` (2014) to `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2024_twh_str` (2024). LBNL projects `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_ref_twh_str` by 2030 in its reference case, within a range of `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_low_value_str` to `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_high_twh_str` [@shehabi2024united; @shehabi2026united], with AI workloads treated as an important driver of growth. At the high end, data centers would consume approximately `{python} UsDatacenterElectricity.us_2030_high_share_str` of US electricity, motivating evaluation of the generation, transmission, and connection capacity needed to serve that projected demand.

figures.title: Operational Carbon Footprint of Large-Scale ML Tasks
figures.caption: **Operational Carbon Footprint of Large-Scale ML Tasks**: Stacked bars show operational CO~2~e over the reported accounting periods for Meta's recommendation models (RM-1 through RM-5), a language model (LM), and several open-source large models (BERT-NAS, Evolved Transformer, T5, Meena, GShard-600B, Switch Transformer, GPT-3). The recommendation-model bars divide roughly evenly between training (light and mid orange) and inference (solid orange), while the public open-source baselines report training-only footprints (hatched gray outline), underscoring that inference serving at scale can rival or exceed training emissions for deployed systems. Direct-to-chip liquid: a cool supply tube rises from heat rejection to a cold plate on the chip, and a warm return tube carries heat back down to heat rejection.

figures.title: AI System Lifecycle
figures.caption: **AI System Lifecycle**: Four stages in sequence, each dropping the burden it adds, with a recovery loop from decommissioning back to manufacture. A dashed line from design runs under all three burden boxes, labeled load set at design time. A dashed green loop labeled refurbish or recover returns from decommission to manufacture.

figures.title: A Feasible Carbon-Aware Schedule
figures.caption: **A Feasible Carbon-Aware Schedule**: Three constraints share one time axis. The capacity lane shows a hatched busy period followed by available headroom. An equation below sums integrated power times carbon intensity with checkpoint, idle, and migration terms.

figures.title: European Electricity Generation over One Week
figures.caption: **European Electricity Generation over One Week**: Hourly public net generation by source for the European Union in week 47 of 2023 (20 to 26 November), stacked, with the load curve on top. Nuclear forms a nearly flat base, hydro follows the daily demand cycle, and solar adds only small midday bulges this late in the year. Wind swings across days rather than hours, from about 27 GW on Sunday to about 111 GW on Thursday, so the fossil gas and coal that fill the remaining gap move from day to day. Lower-carbon windows for deferrable training therefore come from the forecast for a specific week and region, not from a fixed daily pattern. Source: Energy-Charts (Fraunhofer ISE) public power data, from ENTSO-E and national statistics.
figures.alt: Stacked area chart of hourly European Union electricity generation in gigawatts over seven days, 20 to 26 November 2023, with a black load line on top. From bottom to top the bands are nuclear, flat near 70 GW; hydro, rising and falling each day; biomass and other; wind, thin early in the week, widest on Thursday and Friday, and thin again on Sunday; solar, small midday bumps; fossil gas; and coal, lignite, and oil. The wind band is drawn in saturated navy while the other bands are pale tints, and the bands and load line are labeled directly at the right edge, except solar, which is labeled at its Tuesday midday bulge. Brackets on the wind band mark its thinnest hour, 27 GW on Sunday, and its widest, 111 GW on Thursday. Load peaks between about 310 and 365 GW each weekday.

figures.title: Production Responsible AI Architecture
figures.caption: **Production Responsible AI Architecture**: The request path performs access controls, minimization, and inference. In the asynchronous governance lane, the evidence log feeds explanations and parity metrics, the known labels feed error-rate metrics, and all three feed a release gate with a named owner, from which a dashed approved-update arrow returns to inference.

figures.title: Privacy Boundaries in Federated Training
figures.caption: **Privacy Boundaries in Federated Training**: Clients retain raw records and contribute clipped updates through secure aggregation. In this central differential privacy design, a trusted curator receives the aggregate, adds calibrated noise, and accounts for repeated releases before publishing a model. Secure aggregation protects individual updates under its protocol assumptions; differential privacy bounds the released model relative to the specified privacy unit. Neither implies a universal ordering of privacy strength.

figures.title: Model Update Strategies
figures.caption: **Model Update Strategies**: Three approaches to removing a data point's influence. Full retraining gives exact unlearning at the highest cost; gradient ascent provides an approximate update by maximizing loss on the forget set; and SISA training partitions data into shards so only the affected shard is retrained. The accompanying cost model quantifies the full-retraining and SISA cases.
figures.alt: Three panels, each showing the same grid of training-data tiles. Full retraining: every retained tile is shaded as recomputed and the two forget-set tiles are dashed as removed, feeding train from scratch on retained data; guarantee exact, recompute whole model. Gradient ascent: only the two forget-set tiles are shaded as recomputed, feeding an ascent step theta plus eta times the gradient of the loss; guarantee approximate, recompute forget-set passes. SISA sharding: the grid splits into shards S1, S2, and S3; only S3, which held the removed forget-set tiles, is shaded and retrained while S1 and S2 are kept; guarantee exact, recompute one shard, serving by shard vote. A key below names recomputed, untouched, forget set, and forget set removed.

figures.title: Model Interpretability Spectrum
figures.caption: **Model Interpretability Spectrum**: A heuristic ordering by model family. Small linear models and shallow decision trees can offer transparent reasoning, while neural networks typically require post-hoc explanation techniques; size, feature meaning, and audience can move any model along the spectrum. This distinction guides model selection based on application needs, prioritizing transparency in regulated domains or when stakeholder trust is important. The label under each family names the handle an explanation typically uses.
figures.alt: Six model families in a row above a double-headed axis running from more interpretable to less interpretable, each with a small structural sketch whose explanation handle is drawn dark. Sparse linear models: a few nonzero coefficient bars, coefficients. Small decision trees: one highlighted split path, split paths. Prototype and concept models: an input linked to its matching exemplar, exemplars. Tree ensembles: six small trees, each with one dark root-to-leaf path, TreeSHAP. Deep neural networks: dense layers with shaded input nodes, gradients and SHAP. Foundation models: a deep layer stack with a probe reading one layer, probing. Brackets group the first two as interpretable by design, the third as hybrid, and the last three as needing post-hoc explanation.

figures.title: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Alignment Pipeline
figures.caption: **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) Alignment Pipeline**: The top lane carries the policy from a pretrained model through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and proximal policy optimization (PPO) to the aligned policy. The bottom lane turns human judgment into an objective: raters compare sampled SFT outputs, and those comparisons train a reward model whose score drives PPO. The SFT model also serves as the KL reference that limits how far PPO moves the policy, so every human preference reaches the weights only through the learned reward model.
figures.alt: Two lanes. Policy lane: pretrained model, supervised fine-tuning, RL fine-tuning with PPO, and aligned policy, joined by arrows, with a dashed arrow labeled KL reference running over the top from supervised fine-tuning to PPO. Human judgment lane: a stack of human raters feeds a stack of preference pairs, each showing outputs y1 and y2 with y1 preferred, which trains a reward model r of x and y drawn as the one dark filled box. Only two arrows cross between lanes: a dashed arrow labeled sampled outputs from supervised fine-tuning down to the preference pairs, and a heavy arrow labeled reward signal, the only path to weights, from the reward model up to PPO.

figures.title: Reward Hacking Loop
figures.caption: **Reward Hacking Loop**: Maximizing measurable rewards, like clicks, can incentivize unintended model behaviors that undermine the intended goal of user satisfaction. In the illustrated possible feedback loop, the recommender serves content and the resulting clicks enter later training data. If optimizing clicks rewards behavior that undermines long-term user value, retraining can reinforce the mismatch. Establishing this mechanism requires evidence about the deployed policy and the user-value criterion; targeting a proxy does not by itself prove that it has ceased to provide useful information.
figures.alt: A circular loop of four boxes joined by curved arrows: ML recommender, optimizes the proxy, serves served content, clickbait and outrage, which elicits clicks, which are logged as training data, which retrains the recommender. The center of the loop reads loop closes on the proxy. Outside the loop, a proxy metric box, maximize clicks, sends reward down to the recommender, and a true goal box, long-term user value, points to the proxy labeled measured by. A dashed red arrow labeled undermines runs from served content to the true goal.

figures.title: Fairness Monitoring Pipeline
figures.caption: **Fairness Monitoring Pipeline**: End-to-end observability for deployed models. Model predictions feed subgroup metric computation across demographic segments; a threshold check identifies performance or fairness regressions; and alerts initiate investigation and may trigger candidate retraining. Validation and an authorized release decision determine whether an update returns to serving; monitoring alone does not preserve responsible AI properties.
figures.alt: Flow diagram. A predictions card of green record tiles feeds a subgroup gaps card, a small bar chart for groups G1 to G4 against a dashed tolerance line epsilon fair, with delayed matched labels arriving from above. The G3 bar exceeds the line and is red; an arrow labeled exceeds leads to a fairness alert to investigate, then a candidate update to recalibrate or retrain. A green branch from the gaps card reads within, keep serving. The candidate update passes down to validation on subgroup-labeled data, then left to a release gate with an authorized owner, whose dashed approved-update arrow returns to the serving model, which feeds new predictions.

figures.title: Bias Amplification Feedback Loop
figures.caption: **Bias Amplification Feedback Loop**: When ML systems retrain on their own outputs, historical bias in training data propagates through model predictions, downstream outcomes, and reinforced data before feeding back as even more biased retraining data. The edges ('trains on', 'produces', 'creates', 'feeds into') show a possible reinforcing mechanism, not a guarantee that every iteration increases disparity. Green intervention arrows mark where pre-processing (data audit and reweighting), in-processing (fairness constraints), and post-processing (threshold calibration) can break the cycle.

Three green intervention boxes each send an arrow to a green bar that cuts one arc: pre-processing, audit and reweight, cuts the feeds into arc; in-processing, fairness constraints, cuts the trains on arc; post-processing, threshold calibration, cuts the produces arc.

figures.title: Layers of Responsibility
figures.caption: **Layers of Responsibility**: Effective human-centered AI implementation requires shared accountability across nested layers. From the core Development Team outward through the Organization, Industry, and Government/Society, each surrounding layer enforces norms the inner layers cannot self-impose. Each layer's anchor is written into a gap in its own top boundary, so the norm forms part of the wall: GDPR, the EU AI Act, and sector-specific law; ISO standards and external audits; impact assessments and ethical review boards; and fairness testing, model cards, and red-teaming.

figures.title: From Model Serving to Closed-Loop Agentic Fleets
figures.caption: **From Model Serving to Closed-Loop Agentic Fleets**: The dashed outline in each panel is the accounting boundary. For model execution (a), the boundary holds only the forward pass, so FLOPs per token and joules per token describe it. For a complete workflow (b), the boundary holds planning, retrieval, tool execution, verification, and every retry after a failed check, with the model called from inside the loop; a copy of the panel (a) boundary encloses one of those calls. The cost is therefore counted per useful task completed: the unit of account shifts from one token to one verified result. Minimizing that cost requires evaluating the whole loop at the required quality and safety.
figures.alt: Two panels. Panel a, model execution: a prompt box feeds a model forward pass box inside a dashed boundary, which emits a row of token squares, the first filled and labeled 1 unit; the note below reads measured per token, FLOPs per token and joules per token. Panel b, complete workflow: a goal box feeds plan, retrieve, run tool, and verify boxes inside a larger dashed boundary. Small model boxes sit above plan, retrieve, and run tool, and the one above plan has its own small dashed boundary. A red dashed arrow labeled check failed, retry runs beneath the stages from verify back to plan. Verify feeds a green verified result box outside the boundary, labeled 1 unit; the note below reads measured per task, joules per useful task completed.

figures.title: A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop
figures.caption: **A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop**: In the conversational arrangement (A), the model answers and the developer runs every tool and carries each error back by hand. In the agentic arrangement (B), the runtime assembles context, receives the model's proposal, and dispatches only actions it grants; the model holds no authority, and verifier evidence returns to the runtime rather than to the model's own report.
figures.alt: Two panels with the same layout and a dashed line separating the proposing tier above from the acting tier below. Panel A, A person closes the loop: a model endpoint labeled answers only sits above the line; a developer labeled carries everything sits below it, sends prompt plus error up to the endpoint and receives a patch, runs commands in a local terminal, and receives the error back. Panel B, A runtime closes the loop: a foundation model labeled holds no authority sits above the line; an agent runtime labeled grants each action sits below it, sends context up and receives a proposal, dispatches to an isolated sandbox along a violet arrow and receives an observation, and the sandbox feeds verifiers labeled tests, linters, whose evidence returns to the runtime.

figures.title: The Six-Phase Turn Lifecycle
figures.caption: **The Six-Phase Turn Lifecycle**: Each phase marks a change in which component is responsible, not a mandated scheduler. The runtime assembles context, authorizes requests, records outcomes, and assesses progress; the model only proposes, and only an authorized request reaches a tool. A timed-out tool leaves its outcome unknown, and acceptance requires evidence independent of the model's own report, so exhausted limits end in an unresolved outcome or escalation rather than success.
figures.alt: Six phase boxes arranged in a U, each colored and labeled by the component responsible. Top row, left to right: 1 context assembly, runtime; 2 model invocation, model; 3 validate and authorize, runtime, joined by context and proposal arrows. A bold violet authorized arrow descends from phase 3 to the bottom row, which runs right to left: 4 tool execution, tool; 5 observation and evidence, runtime; 6 assess against contract, runtime, joined by outcome and evidence arrows, with a dotted note under the outcome arrow reading unknown if timed out. A dashed red rejected, no execution arrow runs from phase 3 to phase 5 without touching phase 4. Dashed arrows labeled needs approval from phase 3 and wait from phase 6 lead to a dashed wait box labeled resumes, not an exit. A next-turn arrow returns from phase 6 to phase 1, and phase 6 also leads to a green accept deliverable box, evidence meets contract, and a red stop without acceptance box, unresolved or escalate.
figures.systems_goal: Separate turn responsibility, dispatch authorization, waiting, and evidence-based acceptance.

From the stop reason an arrow drops into an agent runtime region to a route on stop reason box. Its tool call branch goes to validate, authorize, then run in sandbox, and from the sandbox an arrow returns up to the tool slab of the request. Its end of turn branch goes to verify, and its output limit branch goes to a red quarantine box.

figures.title: One Keyword, Two Token Sequences
figures.caption: **One Keyword, Two Token Sequences**: The same Python line, unindented and indented by four spaces, drawn on one character grid, with a compiler lexer's tokens above the characters and a byte-pair tokenizer's tokens below. The lexer records indentation as block structure and emits the same keyword and identifier for both lines. The tokenizer absorbs the fourth space into the keyword, so the indented line opens with two tokens that do not appear in the unindented one; only the four tokens after the keyword are shared. Identifiers are from the `cl100k_base` vocabulary.
figures.alt: Two stacked blocks, unindented and indented by four spaces. Each block shows a row of character cells for the line def get_user_id():, with lexer tokens above and byte-pair tokens below, each token spanning the characters it covers. Lexer tokens are def, get_user_id, open parenthesis, close parenthesis, and colon; the indented line adds a dashed indent token over the four spaces. Byte-pair tokens for the unindented line are def 755, space get 636, _user 3398, _id 851, and parentheses colon 4658, labeled 5 tokens. For the indented line they are three spaces 262, space def 711, and the same four tokens, labeled 6 tokens. Tokens 755, 262, and 711 are filled dark; a dashed line marks where the lexer splits the indent from def, which the 711 token straddles. Brackets below mark the two leading tokens, where the fourth space joins the keyword, and the four tokens shared by both lines.

figures.title: Reject, Then Cancel
figures.caption: **Reject, Then Cancel**: The runtime's stream validator advances a parser state as each prefix arrives and holds the output rather than acting on it. At step `{python} StreamCancel.k_cut_str` the proposal introduces a key outside the schema, so the runtime records a rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The runtime outcomes on the left hold regardless of the service; the service outcomes on the right hold only if the service receives and honors the cancel request.
figures.alt: Three lanes. Top, model service: an output allowance bar drawn to scale for 4,096 steps, with a thin solid sliver for the first 96 steps and a long dashed region labeled up to 4,000 decode steps not run. Middle, token stream: a zoom into the sliver shows step 1, an opening brace, step 2, a query key, steps 3 to 95 elided, and step 96, a force key outlined in red. Bottom, agent runtime stream validator: parser transitions q0 to q1 and q1 to q2, each held, and at step 96 a red box marked REJECTED, key not in schema. A red cancel request arrow runs from the rejection up to the dashed region of the allowance bar. Below, runtime outcomes: partial proposal never dispatched, rejection recorded in the envelope, error returned to the model next turn. Service outcomes, if honored: decoding stops at step 96, request leaves the batch, KV cache memory released.

figures.title: Grammar-Constrained Decoding
figures.caption: **Grammar-Constrained Decoding**: A tool schema compiles once into an automaton whose states each carry a token mask. At every step the mask sets illegal tokens to $-\infty$ before normalization, so only a legal continuation can be drawn, and the drawn token advances the automaton. The logit values are illustrative: a fluent but illegal continuation can outscore the legal one and still receive zero probability. A precomputed per-state mask suits a finite-state constraint; nested structures need additional parser state. The strip along the bottom lists what the mask leaves unchecked.
figures.alt: Diagram. Top: a tool schema with query and limit fields compiles into an automaton with states q0, q1, q2, and final state qF, joined by edges labeled opening brace and query. Above each state sits a strip of mask bits; the strips for q0 and q1 show a few legal bits filled, and q0 is highlighted as the current state. A lookup arrow runs from q0 to an operator plus M of q0 between two bar charts. The left chart, logits z_t, shows illustrative scores SELECT +14.2, I think +18.5, opening brace +8.1, and Sure +12.0. The right chart, masked z prime t, shows SELECT, I think, and Sure as dashed outlines marked minus infinity and only the opening brace bar solid at +8.1. The sampled token y_t, an opening brace, feeds an arrow back up to state q1, labeled advance to q1. A dashed strip at the bottom reads not checked by the mask: table exists, values right, call authorized.

figures.title: Committing to a Hypothesis vs. Checking It
figures.caption: **Committing to a Hypothesis vs. Checking It**: Both paths start from the same connection-pool failure. On the left, generation builds on the timeout explanation without any observation that separates it from a missed notification, so the patch can hide the symptom while the defect remains. On the right, a targeted test orders a waiting worker and a returning connection, and its observation contradicts the timeout explanation before any edit. The revised candidate passes the reproducer, which still falls short of task acceptance.
figures.alt: Two lanes below a box reading observed failure, request waits after a connection frees. The left lane, labeled commit first, holds H1 timeout too short with H2 missed notification drawn faded and dashed, then generate on H1 with no new evidence, then a timeout patch applied unchecked, ending in a red box reading symptom masked, notification defect remains. The right lane, labeled check first, holds both H1 and H2, then an amber targeted test observing the waiter still blocked after return, then the hypotheses again with H1 struck through and marked contradicted, then a notify on return patch, the revised candidate from H2, ending in a green box reading reproducer passes, acceptance still pending. A dashed horizontal line labeled first edit crosses both lanes: the left lane reaches it with no check, the right lane only after the test.

figures.title: Stopping Precedence
figures.caption: **Stopping Precedence**: Before admitting more work, the runtime tests three conditions in a fixed order. A hard ceiling on tokens, calls, depth, or time stops new admissions, preserving any already acceptable candidate for the acceptance decision. Within the ceilings, a candidate that meets the acceptance criteria ends search and goes to the acceptance decision, which stopping does not itself make. Only then does the marginal rule compare the gain per unit cost with $\MarginalStoppingThreshold$. A stop without an acceptable candidate is reported as incomplete or escalated, never returned as accepted.
figures.alt: Flowchart. A box reading before admitting more work leads to three diamonds in sequence: 1, hard ceiling reached; 2, acceptance criteria met; 3, gain per cost below epsilon stop. A no from the first two passes to the next diamond. A no from the third leads up to a box reading admit next work, which loops back to the start. Each yes leads down to an outcome card: stop new work, listing tokens, calls, depth, and time and reading keep acceptable candidate, else incomplete or escalate; stop search, reading return the candidate for the acceptance decision; and stop early, reading further work not worth its cost, report incomplete or escalate.

figures.caption: **From Agent Context to KV State**: A 32,768-token agent context (a), divided into system prompt, tool schemas, workspace, turn history, and the latest observation, becomes key and value tensors at every layer (b). A chain of boxes derives 327,680 bytes per token, multiplies by S to reach 10.7 GB per context, and tiles that footprint into the KV pool, where resident fit B equals the floor of the pool size over the per-context footprint and falls as 1 over S.

figures.title: Leaf-First Eviction in a Radix Prefix Cache
figures.caption: **Leaf-First Eviction in a Radix Prefix Cache**: Each node stands for a run of tokens and the KV blocks that hold them, so a request's cached state is the path from the root to its node. Nodes on a running request's path stay active. Only dormant leaves are eligible, which is why the dormant Other-task node in panel (a) survives until its Final-turn child is evicted in panel (b). A least-recently-used policy would choose among the eligible leaves; it never removes an ancestor before its retained descendants.
figures.alt: Two stacked copies of a three-level tree, panel a above panel b, whose nodes each carry a small row of KV block squares. Panel a has an active shared-prefix root, an active repair-history node with an active test-log-turn leaf and a dormant rejected-branch leaf, and a dormant other-task node with a dormant final-turn leaf; thicker green edges trace the running request's path, and the two dormant leaves are shaded gray with dark dashed borders as eligible for eviction. Panel b shows the final-turn leaf faded with dotted borders as evicted and the other-task node now shaded as an eligible dormant leaf. A legend defines active, dormant, eligible, and evicted.

figures.title: Monolithic vs. Chunked Prefill
figures.caption: **Monolithic vs. Chunked Prefill**: Both timelines use the weight-only estimate, on one time axis, for a `{python} ChunkedIteration.prompt_str`-token prefill arriving while `{python} ChunkedIteration.decodes_str` requests decode. Admitted as one unit (a), the prefill separates two decode tokens by about `{python} ChunkedIteration.gap_mono_str`. Split into `{python} ChunkedIteration.chunk_str`-token chunks (b), every iteration also advances the decodes, so the gap is one iteration of about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_iter_str`, and the prompt finishes slightly later. Timeline b has eight equal bars labeled chunk 1 to chunk 8, with a token marker at every bar boundary and a dark bracket over the first bar. Each timeline marks where the prompt completes.

figures.caption: **Searching an HNSW Graph**: Each upper layer holds a geometrically smaller subset of the vectors. The query enters at the top, hops greedily toward $\SearchQueryEmbedding$ until no neighbor is closer, and drops a layer from that node. In layer 0 green links and outlined nodes mark the nodes the beam visited around q and three filled green nodes mark the returned nodes; the remaining gray nodes were never visited. A key identifies greedy hop, visited by beam with width ef search, returned best k, and never visited.

An arrow appends the code to cell C. figures.title: Three Responses to a Source Edit
figures.caption: **Three Responses to a Source Edit**: Synchronous re-indexing blocks the write until r18 entries exist, adding `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_local_str` to `{python} IndexMaintenanceCost.t_serial_str` under the notebook's stipulated costs. Background re-indexing without a generation check returns after the source commit but admits r17 entries as current until the rebuild finishes. Background re-indexing with coordinated exclusion returns before rebuilding finishes; a query in the interval sees r17 excluded and receives a direct read or a partial result, and the worker publishes only if its generation is still current. The cost labels compare incremental indexing and local metadata work, excluding the common durable commit and coordination costs and any fallback retrieval. The time axis is schematic.
figures.alt: Three stacked timelines on a shared time axis marked r18 committed and r18 entries ready, with the shaded refresh window between them; each timeline has rows for agent, worker, and index serves. Synchronous re-index, noted as incremental indexing work of 88 ms (local) to 1.26 s (remote, per file): after edit r18 the agent's write is blocked while the worker parses, updates postings, and embeds r18, the index serves r17 entries until r18 entries are ready, and a later query gets r18. Background re-index with no generation check, noted as rebuild off the write path: during the window a red query bar reads query gets r17 as current while the index row reads r17 admitted as current. Background re-index with exclusion, noted as local metadata work of 0.4 microseconds per write and 1.5 microseconds per query: during the window the index row reads r17 excluded, an amber query bar reads query: direct read or partial, and the worker row ends with publish if current.

figures.title: One operation, many attempts
figures.caption: **One operation, many attempts**: The runtime creates the operation ID once and gives each attempt a fresh attempt ID, so a timeout leads either to another attempt of the same intent or, once attempts run out, to an unresolved outcome. The endpoint's lookup, scoped to caller and resource within its retention window, decides whether a request returns a retained result, a pending status, or an ID conflict, or executes. Only the last branch applies the effect. Recording the result inside the same transaction boundary, where the effect permits one, keeps a crash from leaving an applied effect without the record that deduplicates its retries.
figures.alt: Two-part flow diagram. On the left, a runtime column: admit intent creates the op ID once; attempt k, drawn as a stack of cards, keeps the same op ID with a new attempt ID; a red timeout box with effect unknown loops back to the attempt and leads, dashed, to an unresolved box once attempts are exhausted. A request arrow goes to an endpoint lookup of the op ID scoped to caller, resource, and retention window, and a dashed reply returns. The lookup fans out to four outcomes: completed returns the retained result, still running returns a pending status, payload differs is an ID conflict, and not found executes. A bracket marks the first three as no new effect; only not found continues into a dashed box labeled one transaction, which holds apply effect followed by record result.
figures.systems_goal: Show how repeated attempts avoid repeating one logical effect under an endpoint contract.
storyboard: Create one operation ID and dispatch a first attempt.

Trace endpoint completed, pending, conflict, and unseen branches; only unseen executes.

figures.title: Bounded capture before staging
figures.caption: **Bounded capture before staging**: The adapter drains each bounded pipe from one readiness loop, so neither channel stalls the child, and enforces a byte limit and a deadline on capture. The head fills once, the tail ring overwrites its oldest bytes, and the middle is counted but not kept, so capture memory stays fixed however long the process writes. The staged observation carries status, head, a notice of the measured omission, and tail within the byte budget $\ObservationByteBudget$; a retained record, when authorized, lets later calls read omitted ranges by handle.
figures.alt: Datapath diagram. A child process writes stdout and stderr into an adapter, where both bounded pipes feed one readiness loop labeled byte limit and deadline. The loop emits an output stream of any length, drawn as a bar along a time axis: a head segment, a long hatched middle that is counted but not kept, and a tail segment. Below it, a fixed-size capture memory holds a full linear head buffer, an omission count that keeps no bytes, and a tail ring buffer that overwrites its oldest slots. The buffers feed a staged observation stacked as status, head, a dashed notice of bytes omitted, tail, and handle; below the stack, the equation M obs,max equals M head plus M notice plus M tail, and an arrow leads to the next model call, measured in tokens. A dashed retained record, if authorized, serves range reads to the handle.
figures.systems_goal: Explain bounded tool-output capture without hiding omissions or stalling a child process.

figures.title: Where Each Boundary Acts
figures.caption: **Where Each Boundary Acts**: Two requests steered by the same README text cross mediation, the execution envelope, and egress. The injected `run_shell` request is admitted because it is well typed, then stopped where it tries to read the credential. The dashed segment marks that the destination policy would also refuse its upload, a check on a different part of the path rather than an independent backup. The second request passes every check because each of its steps is permitted, so its disclosure reaches the approved service without any boundary being escaped.
figures.alt: Five columns labeled model proposal, mediation with tool admission, execution envelope with filesystem policy, egress with destination policy, and outside the runtime. Each boundary is drawn as a vertical wall with an opening where a request passes. An injected run_shell request passes the mediation wall, marked admitted, and stops at a solid red block in the execution envelope wall marked read denied; a dashed segment continues to a dashed red block in the egress wall marked upload denied, and a dashed diagnostics box is marked not reached. A submit_report request on the permitted channel passes all three walls, marked admitted, read allowed, and sent, and a red arrow reaches an approved service box marked disclosure.
figures.systems_goal: Distinguish a blocked credential read from harmful disclosure through an allowed channel.
storyboard: Trace the injected shell request through admission to its denied read.

figures.title: Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind
figures.caption: **Attenuation and What It Leaves Behind**: Panel A derives two children from the edit grant. The test grant is rejected because it requests execute, which the parent never held, even though its expiry is earlier. The scan grant is valid because every component is narrower. Deriving it does not remove the edit grant, so a worker that retains the parent can still write until the runtime withdraws it. Panel B shows the chained-caveat alternative, in which each holder narrows a token offline by folding a caveat into the next code, and only a verifier holding the issuer's key can check the whole chain.
figures.alt: Two stacked panels. Panel A, deriving a grant, lists three grants in rows with columns for rights, objects, and expiry. Each row shows read, write, and execute slots, filled where the right is held. The parent Gamma_edit, marked still usable, holds read and write over repo/ with expiry T0 plus 300 s. A dashed red branch derives Gamma_test, marked rejected, which holds read and a red execute slot over repo/ with expiry T0 plus 120 s. A solid branch derives Gamma_scan, marked valid, which holds read only over repo/src/pool.py with expiry T0 plus 120 s. Expiry bars start from a shared T0 line, the parent bar longer than the child bars. Panel B, appending a caveat, shows an issuer holding key k, two holders, and a verifier. The token grows from id and sigma 0, to id, c1, and sigma 1, to id, c1, c2, and sigma 2, beside the formulas sigma 0 equals HMAC of k and id, sigma 1 equals HMAC of sigma 0 and c1, and sigma 2 equals HMAC of sigma 1 and c2, with c1 a prefix repo/src/ and c2 rights read. The verifier recomputes k to sigma 0 to sigma 1 to sigma 2 and checks every caveat.
figures.systems_goal: Show attenuation’s subset rule and why a retained parent grant remains usable.
storyboard: Compare the parent rights, objects, and expiry with both child requests.
Reject the execute expansion and admit the narrower scan without deleting the parent.
Append the pictured caveats and trace verifier recomputation of the chain.

figures.fidelity_guard: Earlier expiry cannot compensate for broader rights; narrowing a copy does not revoke other copies or aggregate budgets. Caption/alt/context review only; artwork not inspected.

figures.title: Where a System Call Lands
figures.caption: **Where a System Call Lands**: Amber boxes run untrusted code, purple boxes are trusted mediators, and the host kernel closes every column. A shared-kernel container sends every call to the host kernel through a filter. A user-space kernel traps and emulates each call and makes a reduced set of host calls. A microVM's guest kernel handles ordinary calls natively, and only device I/O exits to the monitor. Restricted bytecode has no system-call instruction and reaches the host only through imported functions. The columns differ in which interface untrusted code can reach, not in a ranked probability of escape.
figures.alt: Four columns labeled shared-kernel container, user-space kernel, microVM, and restricted bytecode stand on one host kernel bar that spans all of them. A dashed horizontal line marked trust boundary crosses every column, with amber untrusted boxes above it and purple trusted boxes below it. In the container column, an arrow labeled every call, filtered runs from the workload process through a small filter to the host kernel. In the user-space kernel column, the workload process sends every call, trapped, to a user-space kernel that emulates the call and makes reduced host calls. In the microVM column, guest processes make a native system call to a guest kernel inside a dashed guest region, and a VM exit for device I/O crosses the boundary to the monitor with virtual devices, which makes host calls. In the restricted bytecode column, a module with linear memory reaches a runtime with host imports through imported functions only, and the runtime makes host calls for imports.

actual_steps.title: A container still reaches the host
actual_steps.description: The shared-kernel container sends calls through a filter to the host kernel. The filter reduces the exposed interface but does not insert a guest kernel.

actual_steps.title: Emulate calls in user space
actual_steps.description: The user-space kernel traps workload calls and emulates them, issuing a reduced set of host calls itself.

actual_steps.title: Separate a guest kernel
actual_steps.description: The microVM runs native calls against its guest kernel. Device I/O crosses the monitor boundary before host interaction.

actual_steps.title: Expose only imported functions
actual_steps.description: Restricted bytecode accesses host functions through runtime imports and linear memory. The permitted imports define the interface that the host must secure.

figures.title: Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest
figures.caption: **Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest**: The packet filter sees only addresses and ports, so it admits connections to the mediator and drops a direct socket or a lookup sent toward an outside resolver, whatever name the program had in mind. The mediator interprets the request. It resolves its own fixed destinations, admits the repository fetch, and adds the brokered credential, while a push or a request for another repository fails the operation grant at the same hostname. A mediator can inspect or change methods, paths, and bodies only if it makes the upstream request itself or terminates TLS; a proxy that merely forwards encrypted traffic cannot.
figures.alt: Four columns labeled guest with no default route, packet filter that sees addresses and ports, mediator that binds name, operation, and fields, and outside the guest. The packet filter and the mediator are drawn as vertical walls with openings where traffic passes. Four requests leave the guest. A fetch of the approved repo passes the filter to the mediator, is marked fetch admitted with a credential added, and an arrow reaches the approved repository. A push or request for another repo passes the filter to the mediator and stops at a red block in the mediator wall marked operation denied. A direct socket stops at a red block in the filter wall marked dropped, and a dashed metadata host box is marked not reached. A name lookup stops at a red block in the filter wall marked no resolver route, and a dashed external DNS server box is marked not reached.
figures.systems_goal: Separate transport filtering from operation-level egress mediation.
storyboard: Send the approved fetch through the filter to the mediator.
Contrast a same-host unauthorized operation with direct socket and external-DNS attempts.
Highlight where each denial occurs and where the brokered credential is added.

figures.fidelity_guard: A forwarding encrypted proxy cannot inspect paths or bodies; denied routes never reach their illustrated outside targets. Caption/alt/context review only; artwork not inspected.

figures.title: A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse
figures.caption: **A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse**: Instances are restored from a trusted baseline into standby, leased to one trajectory, and marked tainted when the lease ends. Reclaiming then follows the reset contract in order: fence the lease's authority, quiesce owned work, export permitted outputs, discard or restore the covered state, and verify that contract. Passing checks return the instance to standby, and a failed check or an incomplete teardown removes it from service. The checks test a defined contract; a clean scan for known residue does not by itself show that every mutable object was covered.
figures.alt: State diagram. A trusted baseline snapshot is restored into standby, standby is leased to one trajectory, and the leased state ends in tainted, marked not ready for reuse. Tainted leads into a reclaiming container with five ordered steps: fence authority, quiesce owned work, export permitted outputs, discard or restore state, and verify reset contract. A red line from every step joins a red path labeled fails that leads to destroyed, marked removed from service. A green arrow labeled contract checks pass runs from the verify step back to standby.
figures.systems_goal: Make sandbox reuse contingent on a complete reset contract.
storyboard: Restore a trusted baseline, lease it once, then mark it tainted.
Step through fencing, quiescence, permitted export, state reset, and verification.
Return to standby only after checks pass; route any failed teardown to removal from service.
figures.visual: Keep lifecycle state boxes, ordered reclaiming container, green reuse arrow, and red failure join.
figures.fidelity_guard: A clean residue scan is not proof of coverage; guest reset does not reverse external effects or automatically reset attached services. Caption/alt/context review only; artwork not inspected.

actual_steps.title: Lease from a trusted baseline
actual_steps.description: A restored instance begins in clean, unassigned standby before one trajectory leases it. End of that trajectory marks it tainted.

actual_steps.title: Remove authority before reset
actual_steps.description: Reclamation fences authority, quiesces owned work, and exports only permitted outputs before discarding or restoring state. This ordering prevents lingering work from writing into a reused instance.

actual_steps.title: Verify or retire

figures.title: One Sequence, No Enforced Privilege
figures.caption: **One Sequence, No Enforced Privilege**: Application instructions, tool definitions, the user's request, and the README observation become one token sequence in which role markers are ordinary tokens. The README's note can redirect the proposal, and an instruction to treat the README as data is only more advisory input; the release and evidence checks that stop the fixture-bearing search run in the runtime, outside the model.
figures.alt: One row of equal-sized token cells spans the top, grouped under five headers: app instructions from the developer, tool definitions from the runtime, user request from the task owner, a dashed group of advisory cells labeled treat as data, and a README group marked attacker-controlled whose cells are red. Each group except the advisory one starts with a marker token, labeled above as sys, tools, user, or obs, that is drawn exactly like the gray content cells. Thin lines from every cell, red ones from the README cells, converge on a single foundation model box. The model emits a proposed tool call, package_search with a fixture argument, which crosses a dashed model-runtime boundary into a policy check box holding a release check and an evidence check and ending in rejected before dispatch.

figures.title: Three Connections on One Disclosure Path
figures.caption: **Three Connections on One Disclosure Path**: The fixture disclosure needs private data in reach, attacker-controlled content, and an outbound recipient. Each dashed box weakens or removes one connection at some cost to useful work; when the task needs all three, the dependency and recipient check before dispatch decides whether the query may leave. The three connections describe this injection-driven path, not every possible leak or harm.
figures.alt: A single horizontal path runs from a green private fixture box to a red disclosure-at-service box. Between them, wired in series under a bracket labeled all three on one path, are three thick colored links: private data in reach in green, attacker content in red, and outbound recipient in amber, each crossed by a cut mark; the attacker-content link carries a single tick rather than a double cut, because its control only narrows that link. A dashed lead from each cut mark drops to a dashed box naming the control that can weaken or sever that link: protected test runner, result not bytes; quarantined reader, narrows exposure; and egress boundary, no search. After the third link the path passes through a purple dependency plus recipient check labeled before dispatch, and only a dashed red arrow continues to the disclosure.

figures.title: A Quarantined Reader Between Source and Planner
figures.caption: **A Quarantined Reader Between Source and Planner**: The reader extracts a candidate value from the README excerpt with no tools and no credentials. The adapter admits only a completed, schema-valid result, and the runtime attaches metadata from its own ingestion record. The planner sees the claim rather than the raw excerpt, yet a valid claim can still redirect a decision, so every proposal, including one that passes a typed handle, still goes through the reference monitor.
figures.alt: A dashed quarantine zone, labeled no tools and no credentials, encloses a red README box, readme_7, feeding a blue quarantined reader. The only exit from the zone is an arrow to a purple adapter that performs a schema check; a dashed arrow from the adapter leads to a not dispatched box for incomplete or invalid output. The adapter feeds the red reader output section of an admitted record, holding claimed_tests_passed true. A purple runtime ingestion record feeds the record's host metadata section from below, listing record_kind document_claim, source_id readme_7, source_version doc_v3, integrity_provenance untrusted_external, and confidentiality public. The record feeds a blue planner that sees the claim. The planner sends a proposal down to a purple reference monitor showing apply_patch with patch equal to h and resolving h, which also takes input from a handle store holding patch bytes as h. Admitted proposals go down to amber tool adapters.

actual_steps.description: The quarantined reader consumes the README with no tools and no credentials. Isolation removes direct action authority from this extraction step.

actual_steps.title: Validate structure before admission
actual_steps.description: The adapter admits only a completed, schema-valid result. Incomplete or invalid extraction is not dispatched; valid structure alone still establishes no test success.

actual_steps.title: Keep claim and provenance distinct

actual_steps.description: Even apply_patch with a typed handle reaches the reference monitor. The monitor resolves the stored bytes and admits the operation only under the applicable policy.

figures.title: Two Labels, Two Independent Checks
figures.caption: **Two Labels, Two Independent Checks**: A planner invocation that saw both the README and the private fixture yields a query whose integrity provenance $\IntegrityProvenance$ is the union of its inputs' and whose confidentiality $\ConfidentialityLabel$ is their intersection. The search endpoint lies outside $\ConfidentialityLabel(\LabeledRecord)$, so the release check rejects the query before dispatch. Separately, the README-derived test claim lies outside the runner-only $\AcceptedInfluences(\ProposedOperation)$, so the evidence check refuses to record it as a pass.
figures.alt: Three labeled inputs: on the upper left, a red README box with iota equal to readme_7 and kappa equal to every recipient and a green private fixture box with iota equal to fixture and kappa equal to local test runner; along the bottom, a wide red reader extraction box holding claimed_tests_passed: true with iota equal to readme_7. The README and fixture feed a blue planner invocation, which produces a derived query x. Its iota, marked union, holds two chips, a red readme_7 and a green fixture; its kappa, marked intersection, holds one chip, local test runner. A purple reference monitor on the right holds two stacked, independent checks. figures.title: Trajectory State Machine
figures.caption: **Trajectory State Machine**: Five live states, a finalizing state, and three terminal outcomes. The ordinary cycle runs from READY through CALLING_MODEL and WAITING_TOOL back to READY; a proposal that policy requires reviewed is held in AWAITING_APPROVAL, and pause is entered only from READY. Every exit passes through FINALIZING, which stops admission and resolves or transfers remaining duties before an absorbing terminal state. Each arrow is a guarded edge, and events such as a late result or a usage report can update the record's operation table without changing state.
figures.alt: State diagram. A dashed live-states region holds PAUSED above READY, CALLING_MODEL to the right of READY, WAITING_TOOL below READY, and AWAITING_APPROVAL, drawn dashed, below CALLING_MODEL. Heavy arrows trace the ordinary cycle: call admitted from READY to CALLING_MODEL, tool call admitted to WAITING_TOOL, and wait policy met back to READY. Lighter arrows show pause and resume between READY and PAUSED, no admissible action from CALLING_MODEL to READY, approval required from CALLING_MODEL to AWAITING_APPROVAL, approved and guards pass to WAITING_TOOL, and a dashed path for denied, expired, or stale requests returning a refused observation to READY. A completion request arrow and a dashed arrow from any live state for cancel, kill, budget, or deadline lead to FINALIZING, which branches to three double-bordered absorbing states: COMPLETED, FAILED, and CANCELED.

figures.title: Intent Before Dispatch
figures.caption: **Intent Before Dispatch**: The runtime validates a proposal, admits it with a reservation, and waits for the intent's acknowledgment under the declared failure domain before dispatch carries the request past the durability barrier. Where a crash falls determines the recovery state of @tbl-vol3-durable-recovery-states. Before the worker receives the acknowledgment, dispatch is withheld, but the intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost. An absent intent establishes non-dispatch only when the authoritative prefix is complete. Between the acknowledgment and adequate recorded evidence, including a crash before dispatch, the operation is in doubt; a pending or timeout observation leaves it there. After correlated outcome evidence is recorded, the outcome is established within the endpoint's contract.
figures.alt: A row of five ordered event boxes: e prop, proposal; e auth, admission; e flush, intent ack; a ext, dispatch, in amber; and e obs, evidence. A dashed vertical line labeled durability barrier separates e flush from a ext, with runtime can still withhold on its left and request may have left on its right. figures.title: Live Execution vs. Replay
figures.caption: **Live Execution vs. Replay**: In live execution (top), each turn samples the model, passes its proposal through the authorization gate, dispatches the tool, and appends every step to the log. In replay (bottom), the model client is stubbed and tool dispatch is disconnected, so recorded replies and results stream into the harness and any request the log does not account for stops the replay. Folding those events reconstructs the recorded projection, and running harness logic against them is regression replay. A counterfactual branch differs from both, because after restoring its starting state it obtains new observations from compatible fixtures or isolated execution.

Bottom panel, replay: the model, labeled stubbed, and the tools, labeled disconnected, are dashed gray boxes; the link from the gate to the tools ends in a red bar labeled unlogged request: stop; and the same log cells feed a line that streams up into the replaying harness.

figures.title: Recovery Decision Order
figures.caption: **Recovery Decision Order**: Evidence class comes first, because an unknown outcome admits only a retry of the same operation under its repeat contract (a result-recovery probe or a wait gathers evidence that moves the outcome out of this branch rather than acting on it), while a rejected proposal or an established effect opens new proposals, repair, and compensation. Admissibility then removes candidates that lack authority, allowance with the finalization reserve intact, or time; if none remain, the runtime holds or escalates. Expected cost at a matched endpoint chooses only among the admissible survivors, and applies separately to seconds and dollars.
figures.alt: Top-to-bottom flowchart drawn as three stacked horizontal gates crossed by vertical lanes. A box labeled failure evidence recorded leads to gate 1, evidence class, what is known about the effect. Gate 1 feeds two dashed groups: outcome unknown, which covers one lane, and rejected or established, which covers three lanes. All four lanes pass down through gate 2, admissibility, listing authority, allowance with finalization reserve, and deadline; below it the lanes turn dashed and are labeled survivors only. They continue through gate 3, expected cost at a matched endpoint, repair first when p exceeds C repair over C fallback, per axis in seconds and dollars, and the lanes leaving it are labeled ranked by cost. The lanes end in four boxes: retry same operation under outcome unknown, and new proposal, repair using feedback, and compensate under rejected or established. A red arrow labeled none admissible leaves gate 2 on the right and runs down to a fifth box, hold or escalate.

figures.title: Scoped Breaker Transitions
figures.caption: **Scoped Breaker Transitions**: The breaker trips from `CLOSED` to `OPEN` only when the window holds at least $\BreakerMinimumSampleCount$ classified outcomes and their failure fraction reaches $\BreakerTripThreshold$, as in @eq-vol3-breaker-trip. After the cooldown, one probe slot is claimed atomically; only a result from the current generation may close the breaker, while a failed probe reopens it, advances `breaker_generation`, and lengthens the cooldown up to its cap. A late result from an older generation settles its own operation in the operation table and changes no breaker state. Thresholds and cooldowns are policy parameters.
figures.alt: State diagram inside a dashed boundary labeled one dependency scope. Three state boxes: CLOSED, ordinary guards; OPEN, new calls withheld; HALF_OPEN, one probe slot. A red arrow from CLOSED to OPEN is labeled W size at least n min and r at least r trip. An amber arrow from OPEN to HALF_OPEN is labeled T cool elapsed, slot claimed atomically. A green arrow from HALF_OPEN to CLOSED is labeled current-generation probe succeeds. A red arrow from HALF_OPEN back to OPEN is labeled probe fails or times out, advance breaker_generation, lengthen cooldown. Below the boundary, a dotted box, late probe result from an older generation, has a dashed arrow to a box labeled operation table, settles, no transition. Beside it, the update T cool becomes the minimum of twice T cool and T cool max sits above five same-color horizontal bars, labeled per failed probe, with a downward arrow marking successive failed probes; the bars double in length and then stop at a dashed line labeled cap.

figures.title: How Many Tasks an Interval Needs
figures.caption: **How Many Tasks an Interval Needs**: Panel A plots the normal-approximation half-width at 95 percent confidence against the number of independent tasks for three acceptance probabilities. At $\AcceptanceProbability=0.5$, `{python} SampleSizeScale.small_n_str` tasks give about ±`{python} SampleSizeScale.half_small_pp_str` points, and `{python} SampleSizeScale.n_for_target_str` tasks reach the dashed ±`{python} SampleSizeScale.target_pp_str`-point target. Panel B compares Wald and Wilson intervals, in percent, for 50 tasks. With no acceptances, the Wald interval collapses to zero width, while the Wilson upper limit is `{python} PairedAcceptance.zero_upper_str`. With two acceptances, the Wald lower limit falls below zero, an impossible probability. At 25 acceptances the two intervals nearly coincide.
figures.alt: Two panels. Panel A: line chart of normal-approximation half-width in points, from 0 to 20, against independent tasks from 0 to 2,500, with a solid dark curve for p equal to 0.5, a dashed curve for 0.2, and a dotted light curve for 0.05, each labeled at its right end. All three fall steeply and then flatten. Two points on the p equal to 0.5 curve are labeled, 100 tasks at plus or minus 9.8 points and 2,401 tasks where the curve meets a dashed horizontal line at 2 points. figures.title: Verdict-Aware Trace Selection
figures.caption: **Verdict-Aware Trace Selection**: Trace bodies pass a fallible minimization boundary into a bounded buffer that holds them until task verdicts, which can arrive late, reach the selector. Selection applies a declared precedence among the classes of @tbl-vol3-tail-sampling-policies, keeps inclusion probabilities with retained traces, and discards unselected bodies. Every admitted trial also enters the accounting record directly, together with recorded drops, evictions, and truncation, so the denominator does not depend on which bodies survived. Assigning high retention priority protects failure traces under moderate load, though severe buffer saturation can still force evictions before verdicts arrive.
figures.alt: Left-to-right flow diagram. An admitted-trials box sends traces through a dashed amber capture boundary, labeled minimize, redact, into a green bounded buffer drawn as a row of eight slots, some shaded red for failures, some dashed for pending verdicts, one gray, the rest plain, held until verdict. One plain slot drops below the buffer, labeled evicted. The buffer feeds a selection precedence ladder that also receives late task verdicts from above. Its four numbered rungs are failed or violation, shaded red; pending or unknown, dashed; accepted, slow or costly, gray; and ordinary accepted, plain, matching the slot styles. The ladder sends selected traces to a violet trace store that keeps inclusion probability and, from its bottom edge, unselected traces to a dashed discarded box. Along the bottom, a violet evaluation accounting record spans the width, receiving an arrow labeled every trial straight from admitted trials and a red dashed arrow from the evicted slot labeled drops, evictions, truncation.
figures.systems_goal: Preserve evaluation denominators even when bounded trace storage loses incident evidence.

figures.title: Staged Release and Its Hold Path
figures.caption: **Staged Release and Its Hold Path**: Each stage applies its own criterion: the lower bound of the paired acceptance interval against the declared margin offline, a divergence measure of tool-call drift in shadow execution, and a sequential likelihood-ratio monitor with hard tripwires in the canary. The symbols in the stage boxes are defined in the subsections that follow. A wider release requires every criterion of the declared release gate (@eq-vol3-eval-release-gate). An unmet or inconclusive offline result, a drift review that finds a problem, or a canary alarm leads to the same hold. The hold stops new candidate admission; outstanding candidate operations keep their identities and owners, and recovery, not rollback, settles their effects.

Stage 3, canary, holds Lambda sub n versus b sub low and u, a sequential monitor, with red text for hard tripwires. Stage 4, release decision, holds 1 sub ship equals 1, every gate criterion, scoped next step. figures.title: Probes Before Weights
figures.caption: **Probes Before Weights**: Under the default diagnostic route, counterfactual probes evaluate a measured failure in ascending ladder order. A failure that disappears under a probe routes to an immediate systems repair, modifying versioned artifacts that revert cleanly as configuration. Only failures that survive every lower-rung probe reach the weight modification stages, where supervised fine-tuning precedes reinforcement learning. Engineering cost rises and operational reversibility falls from top to bottom.
figures.alt: Flowchart running down a left column from a red measured failure box, recorded failing trace, through three probe boxes: context probe, missing fact supplied; schema probe, rerun with corrected tool description; and runtime probe, clean sandbox, raised limits. Red arrows labeled persists link the probes. From each probe an arrow labeled disappears leads right to a repair box under the heading repair below the weights: repair context, retrieval or assembly; repair tool or schema, schema, docs, or adapter; and repair runtime, bounds, sandbox pool, recovery. A red arrow labeled survives every probe crosses a dashed horizontal boundary to a red residual failure box, plausibly behavioral, which leads on evidence to supervised fine-tuning, curated residual corpus, and then down to reinforcement learning, rollouts, protected reward check, under the heading change the weights. A gray wedge on the far left widens from top to bottom, labeled cheap, reversible at the top and costly, global at the bottom.

figures.title: Collection Credits Across Four Responsibilities
figures.caption: **Collection Credits Across Four Responsibilities**: Each admitted run holds one credit through rollout, capture, staging, and assessment. The credit returns to the pool only when the record reaches a durable disposition or an acknowledged transfer to another bounded owner, such as the review queue. A watermark derived from in-flight work slows dispatch before the pool is exhausted, and a hard limit stops admission when that feedback arrives late.
figures.alt: A vertical credit pool gauge on the left holds ten credit slots, six filled from the bottom and labeled in flight. A red line at the top of the gauge is labeled hard limit, stops admission, and a dashed line two slots below it is labeled watermark, slows dispatch. An arrow labeled acquire leads from the pool to a single bar divided into rollout, capture, staging, and assessment, with a violet bracket beneath it spanning all four segments and a single credit swatch labeled one credit held per run. From the bar, arrows lead to three boxes: dataset publication, derived version; diagnostic pool, or comparison; and review queue, unresolved hold. Dashed violet lines from all three join a return path along the bottom of the figure into the base of the pool, labeled credit returned on durable disposition or acknowledged transfer.

figures.title: Observation Loss Masking
figures.caption: **Observation Loss Masking**: The mask over a simplified view of the serialized repair example that omits the schema request (selected) and its returned schema (context). Of the segments shown, only the corrected tool call and the final response carry $\PositionLossMask_{t}=1$ and receive a direct loss term. The prompt, task, refused proposal, rejection message, and tool result carry $\PositionLossMask_{t}=0$, yet every one of them is still read through attention, so gradients from later selected targets update the parameters that encode it. Selecting only policy responses fits the policy's conditional distribution; unmasking the observations would also ask the same weights to fit the environment's.

The environment lane, labeled p of s t plus 1 given s t and a t, holds the rejection message and the tool result. A loss mask row beneath reads zero for every segment except the corrected tool call and the final response, which are filled and read one. A green attention line runs from those two mask cells back to the first segment, touching every earlier segment, labeled gradients from selected targets reach every earlier segment.

figures.title: Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples
figures.caption: **Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples**: Two independent examples share one buffer. Under an ordinary causal mask (a), every query in the second example scores keys in the first, so the second example can use context it will not have when served. The block-diagonal mask (b) keeps causal scores only inside each example and sets every cross-example entry to $-\infty$ before the softmax, as in @eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention. The boundary offsets define the blocks; whether a kernel also skips the masked blocks is an implementation property.

In panel b, the same lower triangles are shaded, the whole cross-example block is gray and labeled minus infinity, and the key axis carries the boundary offsets 0, s 1, and s 1 plus s 2. A legend defines the score, minus infinity before softmax, and cross-example score.

figures.title: Exposure Bias and On-Policy Labeling
figures.caption: **Exposure Bias and On-Policy Labeling**: Training only on recorded reference states (a) leaves any state the learner reaches after a deviation without a recorded correction, and the applicable bound, @eq-vol3-quadratic-derivation, grows with $\TurnHorizon^2\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate$. Each labeling round (b) runs the current policy, mixed with the reference at probability $\ReferenceMixingProbability_k$, labels the states it visits, keeps a label only if the sandbox continuation passes the verifier, aggregates, and retrains. A fault-injected record masks the injected error and selects the diagnosis and corrective call. The bound in @eq-vol3-linear-regret-bound applies only when error is measured on learner states and each deviation's disadvantage is bounded by $\DeviationDisadvantage$; aggregation broadens coverage but does not by itself make the training and learner distributions equal.
figures.alt: Two stacked panels. Panel a shows a chain of states s 1, s 2, s 3 through s H inside a dashed band labeled states in the corpus. A red arrow labeled learner deviates leaves the band at s 2 and reaches three dashed red states that drift further from the band, labeled no recorded correction. Beside it, a box labeled reference-state bound gives J of pi minus J of pi star at most the minimum of H and H squared epsilon E. Panel b shows a loop of six boxes: run pi k with reference probability lambda k, visited states, labeler proposes, sandbox verifier, aggregate with D k plus 1 equal to D k union new, and retrain pi k plus 1, with a next round arrow back to the start and a dashed discard arrow below the verifier. A fault-injected record of injected error with mask zero, diagnosis with mask one, and corrective call with mask one feeds the visited states. A box labeled learner-state bound, with the condition disadvantage at most u, gives the minimum of H and u H epsilon pi.
